problems.text: A certain TTL gate has the following values for its logic levels: VOH = 3.6 V, VOL = 0.4 V, VI H = 2.0 V, VI L = 0.8 V. What are the noise margins for this TTL gate?

Suppose the waveforms in Fig. 6.5 are those of an ECL gate with VL = −2.6 V and VH = −0.6 V, and t1 = 100 ns, t2 = 105 ns, t3 = 150 ns, and t4 = 153 ns. What are the values of V10%, V90%, V50%, tr, and tf ?
(a) What is the power-delay product at low power for the logic gate characterized by Fig. 6.6? (b) What is the PDP at P = 3 mW? (c) At 20 mW?
(a) Calculate the power supply current I DD if the voltage at node Y is 203 mV. (b) Repeat for 132 mV. (c) Repeat for 64.4 mV.
What is the dynamic power dissipated by alternately charging and discharging a 1-pF capacitor between 2.5 V and 0 V at a frequency of 32 MHz? At 3.2 GHz?

Suppose vI = 1 V for the CMOS inverter in Fig. 7.4. (a) What is the range of values of vO for which MN is saturated and MP is in the triode region? (b) For which values are both transistors saturated? (c) For which values is MP saturated and MN in the triode region?
The (W/L) N of MN in Fig. 7.4 is 10/1. What is the value of (W/L) P required to form a symmetrical inverter?

Equate the expressions for the drain currents of MN and MP to show that vO = vI occurs for a voltage equal to VDD/2 in a symmetrical inverter. What voltage corresponds to vO = vI in an inverter with KR = 10 and VDD = 4 V? For KR = 0.1 and VDD = 4 V?
What is the value of KR for a CMOS inverter in which (W/L) P = (W/L) N? Calculate the noise margins for this value of KR with VDD = 2.5 V, VT N = 0.6 V, and VT P = −0.6 V.
Calculate the average propagation delay of the reference inverter in Fig. 7.12 for C = 1 pF. Repeat for C = 0.2 pF.
An inverter must drive a 5-pF load capacitance with τ p = 1 ns. Scale the reference inverter to achieve this delay.
What would be the W/L ratios in Ex. 7.1 if the threshold voltages of the transistors were +0.5 V and −0.5 V?
What are the new equations [similar to Eqs. (7.16) and (7.17)] for τ PH L and τ PLH for VDD = 2.5 V, VT N = 0.6 V, and VT P = −0.6 V?
problems.answer: τ PH L = 2.4RonnC = 1.26C/Kn; τ PLH = 2.4RonpC = 1.26C/K p

problems.text: What are the new equations [similar to Eqs. (7.16) and (7.17)] for τ PH L and τ PLH for VDD = 3.3 V, VT N = 0.75 V, and VT P = −0.75 V?
problems.answer: τ PH L = 2.4RonnC = 0.94C/Kn; τ PLH = 2.4RonpC = 0.94C/K p

problems.text: (a) What is the power-delay product for the symmetrical reference inverter in Fig. 7.12 operating from VDD = 2.5 V and driving an average load capacitance of 100 fF? (b) Repeat for a 3.3-V supply. (c) Repeat for a 1.8-V supply.

problems.text: (a) What input bias point should be chosen for the amplifier in Fig. 10.13 to provide the maximum possible linear input signal magnitude? What are the maximum input and output signal amplitudes? (b) What is the voltage gain if the amplifier input is biased at VID = −1.0 V?
Write an expression for vO(t) for the amplifier in Fig. 10.13 if vID(t) = (0.25 + 0.75 sin 1000πt) V. What dc bias appears as part of the output voltage?
Suppose an amplifier is operating with vo = +10 V. What is the input voltage vid if (a) A = 100? (b) A = 10,000? (c) A = 120 dB?
Find Av, vo, ii, and io for the amplifier in Fig. 10.19 if R1 = 68 kΩ, R2 = 360 kΩ, and vi = 0.5 V.
If VI = 2 V, R1 = 4.7 kΩ, and R2 = 24 kΩ, find I I , I2, I O, and VO in Fig. 10.19. Why is the symbol VI being used instead of vi, and so on?
problems.answer: 0.426 mA, 0.426 mA, −0.426 mA, −10.2 V; the problem is stated specifically in terms of dc values.

problems.text: We wish to convert a 25-μA sinusoidal current to a voltage with an amplitude of 5 V using a transresistance amplifier. What value of R2 is required? If ii = 50 sin 2000πt μA, what is the amplifier output voltage?
What are the voltage gain Av, output voltage vo, and output current io for the amplifier in Fig. 10.22 if R1 = 2 kΩ, R2 = 36 kΩ, and vI = −0.2 V?
What are the voltage gain in dB and the input resistance of the amplifier shown here? If vi = 0.25 V, what are the values of vo and io? vi vo io 1 kΩ 39 kΩ 100 kΩ R3 R2 R1
Design a noninverting amplifier (choose R1 and R2 from Appendix A) to have a gain of 54 dB, and the current io ≤0.1 mA when vo = 10 V.
problems.answer: Two possibilities of many: (220 Ω and 110 kΩ) or (200 Ω and 100 kΩ)

problems.text: What are the voltage gain Av, input resistance Rin, output voltage vo, and output current io for the amplifiers in Ex. 10.6 if R1 = 1.5 kΩ, R2 = 30 kΩ, and vi = 0.15 V?
Add a resistor to the noninverting amplifier circuit to change its input resistance to 2 kΩ.
problems.answer: Set resistor R3 = 2 kΩ in the schematic on page 548.

problems.text: What is the summing amplifier output voltage vo in Fig. 10.24 if v1 = 2 sin 1000πt V, v2 = 4 sin 2000πt V, R1 = 1 kΩ, R2 = 2 kΩ, and R3 = 3 kΩ? What are the input resistances presented to sources v1 and v2? What is the current supplied by the op amp output terminal?
problems.answer: (−6 sin 1000πt −6 sin 2000πt) V; 1 kΩ, 2 kΩ; (−2 sin 1000πt −2 sin 2000πt) mA

problems.text: Suppose A = 10^5, β = 1/100, and vi = 100 mV. What are A^Ideal v , T, Av, vo, and vid for the noninverting amplifier.
problems.answer: 100, 99.9, 10.0 V, 100 μV (vid is small but nonzero)

problems.text: What value of open-loop gain is guaranteed for the OP-27 op amp over the full temperature range with a load resistance of at least 2 kΩ?

A noninverting amplifier is designed with R1 = 1 kΩ, R2 = 39 kΩ, and an op amp with an open-loop gain of 80 dB. What are the loop gain, closed-loop gain, ideal gain and fractional gain error of the amplifier?
What value of open-loop gain is required to achieve an output resistance of 0.1 Ω in the amplifier in Ex. 11.2.

A noninverting amplifier must have a closed-loop gain of 40 dB and an output resistance of less than 0.1 Ω. The only op amp available has an output resistance of 200 Ω. What is the minimum open-loop gain of the op amp that will meet the requirements?

Suppose a noninverting amplifier has Rid = 1 MΩ, with R1 = 10 kΩ, R2 = 390 kΩ, and the open-loop gain is 80 dB. What is the input resistance of the overall amplifier? What are the currents I−and I1 for a dc input voltage VI = 1 V? Is I−≪I1?
Find the input resistance Rin of an inverting amplifier that has R1 = 1 kΩ, R2 = 100 kΩ, Rid = 1 MΩ, and A = 100 dB. What is the deviation of Rin from its ideal value?
problems.answer: 1001 Ω; 1 Ω out of 1000 Ω or 0.1 percent

problems.text: (a) What is the actual output voltage in the circuit in Fig. 11.31(b) if Vos = 1 mV and A = 60 dB? (b) Calculate the output voltage for the circuit in Fig. 11.31(a).
Repeat the calculation in Ex. 11.10 if the noninverting amplifier gain is set to 50 and the offset voltage is 2 mV?
An inverting amplifier is designed with R1 = 1 kΩ and R2 = 39 kΩ. What value of resistance should be placed in series with the noninverting input terminal for bias current compensation?
problems.answer: 975 Ω. Note that 1 kΩ is the closest 5 percent resistor value.

problems.text: An integrator has R = 10 kΩ, C = 100 pF, VOS = 1.5 mV, and I B2 = 100 nA. How long will it take vO to saturate (reach VCC or VEE) after the power supplies are turned on if VCC = VEE = 15 V?
What is the maximum guaranteed value for the output current of the OP-27A operational amplifier (see MCD website for specification sheets)?

Design a noninverting amplifier to have a gain of 20 dB and to develop a peak output voltage of at least 20 V when connected to a load resistance of at least 5 kΩ. The op amp output current specification states that the output current must be less than 5 mA. Choose acceptable values of R1 and R2 from the table of 5 percent resistor values in Appendix A.
problems.answer: Some possibilities: 27 kΩ and 3 kΩ; 270 kΩ and 30 kΩ; 180 kΩ and 20 kΩ; but not 18 kΩ and 2 kΩ because of tolerances.

problems.text: The CMRR specification of 80 dB in Example 11.12 actually corresponds to −10^4 ≤ CMRR ≤+10^4. What range of output voltages may occur?
What is the voltage gain in Ex. 11.13 if the CMRR is improved to 80 dB? If the differential-mode gain were only 60 dB?
An op amp has a gain of 100 dB at dc and a unity-gain frequency of 5 MHz. What is fB? Write the transfer function for the gain of the op amp.

An op amp has a dc gain of 90 dB and a unity-gain frequency of 5 MHz. What is the cutoff frequency of the op amp? If the op amp is used to build a noninverting amplifier with a closed-loop gain of 40 dB, what is the bandwidth of the feedback amplifier? Write an expression for the transfer function of the op amp. Write an expression for the transfer function of the noninverting amplifier.

An op amp has a dc gain of 90 dB and a unity-gain frequency of 5 MHz. What is the cutoff frequency of the op amp? If the op amp is used to build an inverting amplifier with a closed-loop gain of 50 dB, what is the bandwidth of the feedback amplifier? Write an expression for the transfer function of the op amp. Write an expression for the transfer function of the inverting amplifier.

An op amp has a dc gain of 100 dB and a unity-gain frequency of 10 MHz. What is the upper-cutoff frequency of the op amp itself? If the op amp is used to build a noninverting amplifier with a closed-loop gain of 60 dB, what is the bandwidth of the feedback amplifier? Write an expression for the transfer function of the op amp. Write an expression for the transfer function of the noninverting amplifier.

Suppose that an op amp has a slew rate of 0.5 V/μs. What is the largest sinusoidal signal amplitude that can be reproduced without distortion at a frequency of 20 kHz? If the amplifier must deliver a signal with a 10-V maximum amplitude, what is the full-power bandwidth corresponding to this signal?

problems.text: A particular interconnection between two logic gates in an IC chip runs one-half the distance across a 7.5-mm-wide die. The interconnection line is insulated from the substrate by silicon dioxide. If the line is 1.5 μm wide and the oxide (εox = 3.9εo and εo = 8.85 × 10^−14 F/cm) beneath the line is 1 μm thick, what is the total capacitance of this line assuming that the capacitance is three times that predicted by the parallel plate capacitance formula? Assume that the silicon beneath the oxide represents a conducting ground plane.
problems.how: C = εox·L·W/tox with L = 3.75 mm, W = 1.5 μm, tox = 1 μm, then ×3.

problems.text: Calculate the values of K ^(′) n and K ′ p for NMOS and PMOS transistors with a gate oxide thickness of 10 nm and 5 nm. Assume that μn = 500 cm^2/V · s, μp = 200 cm^2/V · s, and the relative permittivity of the gate oxide is 3.9. (ε0 = 8.854 × 10^−14 F/cm).
problems.how: K′ = μ·Cox″ with Cox″ = εox/tox, εox = 3.9·8.854×10⁻¹⁴ F/cm, 1 nm = 10⁻⁷ cm.

problems.text: (a) The n-well in a CMOS process covers an area of 1 cm × 0.5 cm, and the junction saturation current density is 500 pA/cm^2. What is the total leakage current of the reverse-biased well? (b) Suppose the drain and source regions of the NMOS and PMOS transistors are 2 μm × 5 μm, and the saturation current density of the junctions is 100 pA/cm^2. If the chip has 20 million inverters, what is the total leakage current due to the reverse-biased junctions when vO = 2.5 V? Assume VDD = 2.5 V and VSS = 0 V. (c) When vO = 0 V?
answer: (b) vO = 2.5 V: one reverse-biased junction per inverter (NMOS drain)
(c) vO = 0 V: the PMOS drain is the reverse-biased junction
problems.how: I = J·A; per inverter one 2 μm × 5 μm drain junction is reverse biased; × 20 million inverters.
assume: The n-well of part (a) is counted separately; the totals with the well are shown in brackets.

problems.text: A particular interconnection between two logic gates in an IC chip runs one-half the distance across a 10-mm-wide die. If the line is 1 μm wide and the oxide (εr = 3.9, ε0 = 8.854 × 10^−14 F/cm) beneath the line is 1 μm thick, what is the total capacitance of this line, assuming that the capacitance is three times that predicted by the parallel plate capacitance formula? Assume that the silicon beneath the oxide represents a conducting ground plane.
problems.how: C = εox·L·W/tox with L = 5 mm, W = 1 μm, tox = 1 μm, then ×3.

problems.text: (a) Calculate the voltage at which vO = vI for a CMOS inverter with Kn = K p. (Hint: Always remember that iDN = iDP.) Use VDD = 2.5 V, VT N = 0.6 V, VT P = −0.6 V. (b) What is the current IDD from the power supply for vO = VI if (W/L)N = 2/1? (c) Repeat the calculation in (a) for a CMOS inverter with Kn = 2.5K p. (d) What is the current IDD from the power supply for vO = VI if (W/L)N = 2/1?
problems.how: KR = Kn/Kp; vO = vI where both devices are saturated: vI = (VDD + VTP + VTN√KR)/(1 + √KR); IDD = (Kn/2)(vI − VTN)² with Kn = K′n·2 = 200 μA/V².
assume: K′n = 100 μA/V² (Table 7.1).

(b) Suppose the drain and source regions of the NMOS and PMOS transistors are each 0.5 μm × 1.25 μm in size, and the saturation current density of the junction is 150 pA/cm^2. If the chip has 200 million inverters, what is the total leakage current when vO = 2.5 V? Assume VDD = 2.5 V. (b) Repeat for vO = 0 V.
answer: (b) vO = 2.5 V: reverse-biased NMOS drain junctions
(c) vO = 0 V: reverse-biased PMOS drain junctions

problems.text: A high-speed CMOS microprocessor has a 64-bit address bus and performs a memory access every 2 ns. Assume that all address bits change during every memory access and that each bus line represents a load of 25 pF. (a) How much power is being dissipated by the circuits that are driving these signals if the power supply is 2.5 V? (b) Repeat for 3.3 V.
problems.how: P = N·C·VDD²·f with f the full switching cycle rate: each line changes at every 2 ns access, so a charge-discharge cycle lasts 4 ns (f = 250 MHz).

If L = 1 μm, estimate the area of the transistor.

problems.how: Each switching gate dissipates PDP/τ; 0.2 × 10⁸ gates × PDP/τ ≤ 40 W.

problems.text: What is the minimum logic swing ∆V required for an ECL gate to have a noise margin of 0.1 V at room temperature?

problems.text: Suppose that an ECL gate is to be designed to operateoverthe−55^(°)Cto+75^(°)Ctemperaturerangeand must maintain a minimum noise margin of 0.1 V over that full range. What is the value of the logic swing of this ECL gate at room temperature?

27 °C: VT = 25.86 mV, ΔV needed for NM = 0.1 V
75 °C: VT = 30.0 mV, ΔV needed for NM = 0.1 V
ΔV ≥ 0.4128 V (set by the hottest case, +75 °C)

problems.text: The input signal to an audio amplifier is described by vI = (0.5 + 0.25 sin 1200πt) V, and the output is described by vO = (2 + 4 sin 1200πt + 0.8 sin 2400πt + 0.4 sin 3600πt) V. What is the voltage gain of the amplifier? What order harmonics are present in the signal? What is the total harmonic distortion in the output signal?
answer: 2nd (1200 Hz) and 3rd (1800 Hz) harmonics; fundamental 600 Hz
problems.how: Gain = amplitude of the 600 Hz output component / input amplitude (the dc terms are not part of the gain). THD checked with an FFT of the waveform.

problems.text: The input signal to an audio amplifier is a 1-kHz sine wave with an amplitude of 4 mV, and the output is described by vO = (5 sin 2000πt + 0.5 sin 6000πt +0.20 sin 10,000πt) V. What is the voltage gain of the amplifier? What order harmonics are present in the signal? What is the total harmonic distortion in the output signal?
answer: 3rd (3 kHz) and 5th (5 kHz); only odd harmonics
problems.how: Gain = 5 V/4 mV at 1 kHz; THD = √(0.5² + 0.2²)/5 checked with an FFT.

problems.text: Suppose the VTC for an amplifier is described by vO = 10 tanh (2vI) volts. (a) Plot the VTC. (b) Calculate the distortion based upon the first three frequency components in the output if vI = 0.75 sin 2000πt volts. 10.7 The Differential Amplifier Model

problems.how: Fourier components of 10·tanh(1.5·sin ωt) found with an FFT and by direct integration; THD = √(V2² + V3²)/V1. The plot of part (a) is not reproduced.

assume: R1 = 100 Ω would need R1 + R2 ≈ 19.95 kΩ, just under the limit, so 110 Ω is used.

problems.text: Design an inverting amplifier with Av = 43 dB that can deliver ±15 V to a 5-kΩ load resistor. Your op amp can supply only 4 mA of output current. Use standard resistor 5 percent values in your design. What is the gain of your design?

problems.text: (a) Design a single-stage inverting amplifier with a gain of 46 dB using an operational amplifier. The input resistance should be as low as possible while achieving the op amp output drive capability mentioned here. The amplifier must be able to produce the signal vo = (10 sin 1000t) V at its output when an external load resistance RL ≥5 kΩ is connected to the output of the amplifier. You have an operational amplifier available whose output is guaranteed to deliver ±10 V into a 4-kΩ load resistance. Otherwise, the amplifier is ideal. (b) If the amplifier input signal is vi = V sin 1000t, what is the largest acceptable value for the input signal amplitude V ? (c) What is the input resistance of your amplifier?
answer: (a) R2 (the feedback current must fit in the remaining 0.5 mA)
problems.how: Output guaranteed ±10 V into 4 kΩ → 2.5 mA; the 5 kΩ load takes 2 mA, so 10 V/R2 ≤ 0.5 mA → R2 ≥ 20 kΩ; Rin = R1 = R2/|Av|.

problems.text: (a) A single-pole op amp has an open-loop gain of 100 dB and a unity-gain frequency of 2 MHz. What is the open-loop bandwidth of the op amp? (b) A single-pole op amp has an open-loop gain of 100 dB and a bandwidth of 20 Hz. What is the unity-gain frequency of the op amp? (c) A single-pole op amp has unity-gain-bandwidth product of 30 MHz and a bandwidth of 200 Hz. What is the open-loop gain of the op amp?
problems.how: fT = A0·BW (gain-bandwidth product); 100 dB = 10⁵.

(a) The op amp is used in a noninverting amplifier designed to have an ideal gain of 32 dB. What is the bandwidth of the noninverting amplifier? (b) Repeat for an inverting amplifier with and ideal gain of 32 dB.
problems.how: Single-pole op amp: closed-loop BW = fT·β with β = 1/Av (noninverting) or 1/(1 + |Av|) (inverting).

problems.text: A single-pole op amp has an open-loop gain of 94 dB and a unity-gain frequency of 4 MHz. A noninverting amplifier is needed with bandwidth of at least 20 kHz. (a) What is the maximum closed loop-gain that a noninverting amplifier can have and still meet the frequency response specification? (b) What is the maximum closed loop-gain that an inverting amplifier can have and still meet the frequency response specification?
problems.how: BW = fT/Av (noninverting), fT/(1 + |Av|) (inverting) ≥ 20 kHz with fT = 4 MHz. The open-loop gain (94 dB) only fixes the open-loop bandwidth, 80 Hz.

The op amp is used in an inverting amplifier with an ideal gain of 20. (a) Find an expression for the output impedance of the amplifier. (b) Sketch a Bode plot for the output impedance as a function of frequency.
answer: zero at 250.6 Hz, pole at 238.3 kHz
flat at 262.8 mΩ up to 250.6 Hz, rises 20 dB/decade (inductive) to Ro = 250 Ω at 238.3 kHz, then flat
problems.how: Zout = Ro/(1 + T(s)) with T(s) = A(s)β, A(s) = A0/(1 + s/ωH), β = R1/(R1 + R2) = 1/21 for the inverting gain 20, ωH = ωT/A0.

The op amp is used in a noninverting amplifier with an ideal gain of 20. (a) Find an expression for the input impedance of the amplifier. (b) Sketch a Bode plot for the input impedance as a function of frequency.
answer: Rid(1 + T0 + s/ωH)/(1 + s/ωH) with Rid = 100 kΩ, T0 = 997.6, ωH = 787.3 rad/s (125.3 Hz)
pole at 125.3 Hz, zero at 125.1 kHz
flat at 99.86 MΩ up to 125.3 Hz, falls 20 dB/decade (capacitive) to Rid = 100 kΩ at 125.1 kHz, then flat
problems.how: Zin = Rid(1 + T(s)), T(s) = A(s)β with β = 1/20 for the noninverting gain 20, ωH = ωT/A0.

Write an expression for the output signal. (b) Use the computer to check your answer by plotting the input and output waveforms.
answer: linear in frequency: 10° at 500 Hz, 30° at 1500 Hz, 50° at 2500 Hz (each frequency delayed by the same time 55.6 μs)
problems.how: No waveform distortion needs equal gain and a time delay td constant: phase = −ω·td. At 500 Hz 10° = 360°·500·td gives td = 55.6 μs.
assume: The phase shifts are taken as lags (delays).

R1 = 620 Ω, R2 = 11 kΩ → loss 0.4763 dB, C = 13.56 nF → 13 nF gives fH = 20.86 kHz
problems.how: Loss at low frequency = −20·log₁₀[R2/(R1+R2)] ≤ 0.5 dB gives R2 ≥ 16.9·R1; then C = 1/[2π(R1‖R2)fH].

problems.text: An inverting amplifier is to be designed to have a closed-loop gain of 60 dB. The only op amp that is available has an open-loop gain of 106 dB. What is the tolerance of the feedback resistors if the total gain error must be ≤1 percent? Assume that the resistors all have the same tolerances.
answer: Gain error from the finite open-loop gain alone
problems.how: Worst case: R2 low and R1 high; total gain error = 1 − (Av,actual/Av,ideal) ≤ 1 %, solved numerically with Eq. (11.17). A 0.1 % resistor is therefore adequate.

problems.text: A noninverting amplifier is to be designed to have a closed-loop gain of 54 dB. The only op amp that is available has an open-loop gain of 40,000. What must be the tolerance of the feedback resistors if the total gain error must be ≤2 percent? Assume that the resistors all have the same tolerances. 11.3–11.4 Feedback Amplifier Characterization
answer: Gain error from the finite open-loop gain alone
problems.how: As Problem 11.25 with Av = A/(1 + Aβ), β = R1/(R1+R2); total error ≤ 2 %.

problems.text: An amplifier has an open-loop voltage gain of 100 dB, Rid = 40 kΩ, and Ro = 1000 Ω. The amplifier is used in a feedback configuration with a resistive feedback network. (a) What is the largest value of input resistance that can be achieved in the feedback amplifier? (b) What is the smallest value of input resistance that can be achieved? (c) What is the largest value of output resistance that can be achieved? (d) What is the smallest value of output resistance that can be achieved?
problems.how: Series feedback multiplies a port resistance by (1 + Aβ), shunt feedback divides it by (1 + Aβ); a resistive network cannot give β > 1, so the extremes use β = 1 and Aβ = A = 10⁵.
assume: β ≤ 1 for a passive resistive feedback network.

problems.text: An amplifier has an open-loop voltage gain of 90 dB, Rid = 50 kΩ, and Ro = 5000 Ω. The amplifier is used in a feedback configuration with a resistive feedback network. (a) What is the largest current gain that can be achieved with this feedback amplifier? (b) What is the largest transconductance that can be achieved with this feedback amplifier? 11.5 Voltage Amplifiers—Series-Shunt Feedback
problems.how: Negative feedback can only lower a gain below its open-loop value: for the current amplifier the open-loop (short-circuit) gain is A·Rid/Ro, for the transconductance amplifier A/Ro.

Find the loop gain, ideal voltage gain, actual voltage gain, input resistance, and output resistance for the feedback amplifier.
answer: Loop gain T (return ratio, loading included)
problems.how: Exact nodal analysis of the noninverting circuit with Rid = 30 kΩ, Ro = 5 kΩ, RL = 20 kΩ; T is the return ratio of the dependent source (it includes the loading of Rid, Ro, RL and the feedback network).
assume: The textbook approximates the loaded amplifier by the Section 11.5 two-port method; the exact values are given here.

problems.text: (a) Calculate the sensitivity of the closed-loop input resistance of the series-shunt feedback amplifier with respect to changes in open-loop gain A: (b) Use this formula to estimate the percentage change in closed-loop input resistance if the openloop gain A changes by 10 percent for an amplifier with A = 94 dB and β = 0.01. (c) Calculate the sensitivity of the closed-loop output resistance of the series-shunt feedback amplifier with respect to changes in open-loop gain A: (d) Use this formula to estimate the percentage change in closed-loop output resistance if the openloop gain A changes by 10 percent for an amplifier with A = 100 dB and β = 0.01. 11.6 Transresistance Amplifiers—Shunt-Shunt Feedback

(d) change of Rout for a 10 % change of A
problems.how: Rin = Rid(1 + Aβ), Rout = Ro/(1 + Aβ); differentiate with respect to A.

problems.text: The VTC for an amplifier can be expressed as vo = 15 tanh (1000 vi) V. (a) Use MAT- LAB to find the total harmonic distortion for (a) vi = 0.001 sin 2000πt V. (b) Repeat for vi = 0.002 sin 2000πt V.
problems.how: Fourier series of 15·tanh(1000·vi) found by numerical integration (odd symmetry: only odd harmonics) and checked with an FFT; THD = √(ΣVn²)/V1 up to the 39th harmonic.
assume: The statement asks for MATLAB; the same numbers are computed here with NumPy.

problems.text: A cascade amplifier is to be designed to meet these specifications: Av = 5000 Rin ≥10 MΩ Rout ≤0.1 Ω How many amplifier stages will be required if the stages must use an op amp below? Because of bandwidth requirements, assume that no individual stage can have a gain greater than 50.

assume: Only the gain constraint is evaluated here.

problems.how: The counter runs until the DAC output reaches vX: N clock periods, with N = vX/VFS·2¹² truncated (the DAC output must not exceed vX).
assume: Code obtained by truncation (counting converter stops when the DAC output first exceeds vX).

problems.text: A 20-bit dual-ramp converter is to have an integration time T1 = 0.2 s. How rapidly must the unknown and reference voltage switches change state if this timing uncertainty is to be equivalent to less than 0.1 LSB?
problems.how: A timing error ΔT in T1 is a fractional error ΔT/T1 of full scale; 0.1 LSB = 0.1/2²⁰ of full scale.

problems.circuit: Figure 12–25 (p.621): noninverting amplifier, Rf = 220 kΩ from the output to the inverting input, Ri = 10 kΩ from the inverting input to ground, signal on the + input.

problems.text: Find the values of the input and output impedances in Figure 12–28. Also, determine the closed-loop voltage gain. The op-amp has the following parameters: Aol = 50,000; Zin = 4 MΩ; and Zout = 50 Ω.
problems.how: Inverting amplifier (Floyd §12–5): Zin(I) ≈ Ri, B = Ri/(Ri + Rf), Zout(I) = Zout/(1 + Aol·B), Acl(I) = −Rf/Ri.
assume: BOOK ERROR: the printed solution gives B = 1.0 kΩ/101 kΩ = 0.001, but 1/101 = 0.0099; with B = 0.001 it prints Zout(I) = 980 mΩ. The correct value is 50 Ω/(1 + 50,000 × 0.0099) = 0.101 Ω (an exact KCL solution of the op-amp model confirms it). Still “zero for all practical purposes”.
problems.circuit: Figure 12–28 (p.623): inverting amplifier, Ri = 1.0 kΩ in series with the input to the − input, Rf = 100 kΩ from the output to the − input, + input grounded.

problems.text: Determine Aol for the following values of f. Assume fc(ol) = 100 Hz and Aol(mid) = 100,000. (a) f = 0 Hz (b) f = 10 Hz (c) f = 100 Hz (d) f = 1000 Hz
problems.how: Aol = Aol(mid)/√(1 + (f/fc(ol))²) (Floyd §12–7).
assume: The book prints 99,503 for (b): it truncates 99,503.7.

problems.text: Calculate the phase shift for an RC lag circuit for each of the following frequencies, and then plot the curve of phase shift versus frequency. Assume fc = 100 Hz. (a) f = 1 Hz (b) f = 10 Hz (c) f = 100 Hz (d) f = 1000 Hz (e) f = 10,000 Hz
problems.how: RC lag circuit: θ = −tan⁻¹(f/fc); plot θ against f on a log axis.

problems.text: A certain op-amp has three internal amplifier stages with the following gains and critical frequencies: Stage 1: Av1 = 40 dB, fc1 = 2 kHz Stage 2: Av2 = 32 dB, fc2 = 40 kHz Stage 3: Av3 = 20 dB, fc3 = 150 kHz Determine the open-loop midrange gain in decibels and the total phase lag when f = fc1.
answer: Total phase lag at f = fc1
problems.how: Stage gains add in dB; the phase lags of the stages add: −tan⁻¹(f/fc1) − tan⁻¹(f/fc2) − tan⁻¹(f/fc3).

problems.text: A certain amplifier has an open-loop midrange gain of 150,000 and an open-loop 3 dB bandwidth of 200 Hz. The attenuation (B) of the feedback loop is 0.002. What is the closed-loop bandwidth?
problems.how: Closed-loop bandwidth BWcl = BWol(1 + B·Aol(mid)) (Floyd §12–8).

problems.text: Determine the bandwidth of each of the amplifiers in Figure 12–43. Both op-amps have an open-loop gain of 100 dB and a unity-gain bandwidth ( fT) of 3 MHz.
problems.how: BW(cl) = fT/|Acl| (Floyd Eq. 12–23): (a) Acl = 1 + 220 kΩ/3.3 kΩ = 67.7, (b) Acl = −47 kΩ/1.0 kΩ = −47. The book prints 44.3 kHz and 63.8 kHz.
assume: An exact single-pole solution gives 44.4 kHz and 62.5 kHz (the inverting amplifier's loop attenuation is 1/48 rather than 1/47, so the textbook value is about 2 % high).
problems.circuit: Figure 12–43 (p.635): (a) noninverting amplifier with Rf = 220 kΩ and Ri = 3.3 kΩ; (b) inverting amplifier with Rf = 47 kΩ and Ri = 1.0 kΩ.

problems.text: When a pulse is applied to an op-amp, the output voltage goes from −8 V to +7 V in 0.75 μs. What is the slew rate?
problems.ctx: Example 12–2: The output voltage of a certain op-amp appears as shown in Figure 12–12 in response to a step input. Determine the slew rate.
problems.how: ΔVout = +7 V − (−8 V) = 15 V in 0.75 μs.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.12 Related Problem of Example 12–2, p.610 (PDF 628)

problems.text: If Rf in Figure 12–18 is increased to 150 kΩ, determine the closed-loop gain.
problems.ctx: Example 12–3: Determine the closed-loop voltage gain of the amplifier in Figure 12–18.
problems.how: Noninverting amplifier: Acl(NI) = 1 + Rf/Ri with Rf = 150 kΩ and Ri = 4.7 kΩ (read from Figure 12–18); the example gives 22.3 for Rf = 100 kΩ.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.12 Related Problem of Example 12–3, p.616 (PDF 634)
problems.circuit: Figure 12–18 (p.616): noninverting amplifier, Rf = 100 kΩ from the output to the inverting input, Ri = 4.7 kΩ from the inverting input to ground, signal on the + input.

problems.text: If Ri is changed to 2.7 kΩ in Figure 12–22, what value of Rf is required to produce a closed-loop gain with an absolute value of 25?
problems.ctx: Example 12–4: Given the op-amp configuration in Figure 12–22, determine the value of Rf required to produce a closed-loop voltage gain of −100.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.12 Related Problem of Example 12–4, p.619 (PDF 637)
problems.circuit: Figure 12–22 (p.618): inverting amplifier, Ri = 2.2 kΩ in series with the input to the − input, feedback resistor Rf (unknown) from the output to the − input, + input grounded.

problems.text: (a) Determine the input and output impedances in Figure 12–25 for op-amp datasheet values of Zin = 3.5 MΩ, Zout = 82 Ω, and Aol = 135,000. (b) Find Acl.
problems.ctx: Example 12–5: (a) Determine the input and output impedances of the amplifier in Figure 12–25. The op-amp datasheet gives Zin = 2 MΩ, Zout = 75 Ω, and Aol = 200,000. (b) Find the closed-loop voltage gain.
problems.how: Same circuit as Example 12–5 (Rf = 220 kΩ, Ri = 10 kΩ, so B = 0.0435) with the new op-amp values.
assume: Exact nodal solution: Zin = 20.5 GΩ, Zout = 14.0 mΩ.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.12 Related Problem of Example 12–5, p.622 (PDF 640)
problems.circuit: Figure 12–25 (p.621): noninverting amplifier, Rf = 220 kΩ from the output to the inverting input, Ri = 10 kΩ from the inverting input to ground, signal on the + input.

problems.text: Determine the input and output impedances and the closed-loop voltage gain in Figure 12–28. The op-amp parameters and circuit values are as follows: Aol = 100,000; Zin = 5 MΩ; Zout = 75 Ω; Ri = 560 Ω; and Rf = 82 kΩ.
problems.ctx: Example 12–7: Find the values of the input and output impedances in Figure 12–28. Also, determine the closed-loop voltage gain. The op-amp has the following parameters: Aol = 50,000; Zin = 4 MΩ; and Zout = 50 Ω.
problems.how: Same method as Example 12–7 with Ri = 560 Ω and Rf = 82 kΩ.
assume: Exact nodal solution: Zin = 560.8 Ω, Zout = 110.0 mΩ.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.12 Related Problem of Example 12–7, p.624 (PDF 642)
problems.circuit: Figure 12–28 (p.623): inverting amplifier, Ri = 1.0 kΩ in series with the input to the − input, Rf = 100 kΩ from the output to the − input, + input grounded.

problems.text: Find Aol for the following frequencies. Assume fc(ol) = 200 Hz and Aol(mid) = 80,000. (a) f = 2 Hz (b) f = 10 Hz (c) f = 2500 Hz
problems.ctx: Example 12–8: Determine Aol for the following values of f. Assume fc(ol) = 100 Hz and Aol(mid) = 100,000. (a) f = 0 Hz (b) f = 10 Hz (c) f = 100 Hz (d) f = 1000 Hz
problems.how: Aol = Aol(mid)/√(1 + (f/fc(ol))²).
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.12 Related Problem of Example 12–8, p.630 (PDF 648)

problems.text: At what frequency, in this example, is the phase shift 60°?
problems.ctx: Example 12–9: Calculate the phase shift for an RC lag circuit for each of the following frequencies, and then plot the curve of phase shift versus frequency. Assume fc = 100 Hz. (a) f = 1 Hz (b) f = 10 Hz (c) f = 100 Hz (d) f = 1000 Hz (e) f = 10,000 Hz
problems.how: θ = −tan⁻¹(f/fc) = −60° ⇒ f = fc·tan 60°.
assume: fc = 100 Hz, as in Example 12–9.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.12 Related Problem of Example 12–9, p.631 (PDF 649)

problems.text: The internal stages of a two-stage amplifier have the following characteristics: Av1 = 50 dB, Av2 = 25 dB, fc1 = 1500 Hz, and fc2 = 3000 Hz. Determine the open-loop midrange gain in decibels and the total phase lag when f = fc1.
problems.ctx: Example 12–10: A certain op-amp has three internal amplifier stages with the following gains and critical frequencies: Stage 1: Av1 = 40 dB, fc1 = 2 kHz Stage 2: Av2 = 32 dB, fc2 = 40 kHz Stage 3: Av3 = 20 dB, fc3 = 150 kHz Determine the open-loop midrange gain in decibels and the total phase lag when f = fc1.
answer: Total phase lag at f = fc1
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.12 Related Problem of Example 12–10, p.633 (PDF 651)

problems.text: Determine the bandwidth of each of the amplifiers in Figure 12–43. Both op-amps have an Aol of 90 dB and a unity-gain bandwidth of 2 MHz.
problems.ctx: Example 12–12: Determine the bandwidth of each of the amplifiers in Figure 12–43. Both op-amps have an open-loop gain of 100 dB and a unity-gain bandwidth ( fT) of 3 MHz.
problems.how: Same amplifiers as Example 12–12 (Figure 12–43) with fT = 2 MHz; BW = fT/|Acl|. The open-loop gain (90 dB) only needs to exceed the closed-loop gain.
assume: Exact single-pole solution: 29.6 kHz and 41.7 kHz.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.12 Related Problem of Example 12–12, p.636 (PDF 654)
problems.circuit: Figure 12–43 (p.635): (a) noninverting amplifier with Rf = 220 kΩ and Ri = 3.3 kΩ; (b) inverting amplifier with Rf = 47 kΩ and Ri = 1.0 kΩ.

problems.text: Given that Rf = 100 kΩ; Ri = 2 kΩ; Aol = 120,000; Zin = 2 MΩ; and Zout = 60 Ω, what are Zin(I) and Zout(I) for an inverting amplifier configuration?
problems.how: Inverting amplifier (Floyd §12–4): Zin ≈ Ri; Zout(I) = Zout/(1 + B·Aol) with B = Ri/(Ri + Rf).
assume: Exact nodal solution gives Zin = 2.001 kΩ (the approximation Zin ≈ Ri is what the book uses).

problems.text: The upper critical frequency of a particular op-amp is 100 Hz. What is its open-loop 3 dB bandwidth?
problems.how: For a single-pole response starting at 0 Hz the open-loop 3 dB bandwidth equals the upper critical frequency fc(ol).
assume: The op-amp response is low-pass down to dc, so the bandwidth is fc(ol).

problems.text: If the individual stage gains of an op-amp are 20 dB and 30 dB, what is the total gain in decibels?
problems.how: Stage gains in dB add.

problems.text: If the individual phase lags are −49° and −5.2°, what is the total phase lag?
problems.how: Phase lags of the stages add: −49° + (−5.2°).

problems.text: A certain op-amp is used in a feedback configuration having a gain of 30 and a bandwidth of 100 kHz. If the external resistor values are changed to increase the gain to 60, what is the new bandwidth?
problems.how: Gain × bandwidth is constant: 30 × 100 kHz = 3 MHz, so at a gain of 60 the bandwidth is 3 MHz/60.
assume: The op-amp has a single-pole response (constant gain–bandwidth product).

The answers were computed by this site with the book's own formulas and re-checked by an independent route; for the Examples the result is also compared with the worked solution printed in the book. A Related Problem is shown with the statement of the Example it builds on. The time limit is an assumption (6 minutes per exercise).

problems.text: In Figure 12–28, if Rf is changed from 100 kΩ to 68 kΩ, the feedback attenuation will (a) increase (b) decrease (c) not change
answer: Feedback attenuation B = Ri/(Ri + Rf): 100 kΩ → 68 kΩ
problems.how: B = Ri/(Ri + Rf) with Ri = 1.0 kΩ: a smaller Rf makes the divider ratio larger (0.0099 → 0.0145).
problems.circuit: Figure 12–28 (p.623): inverting amplifier, Ri = 1.0 kΩ in series with the input to the − input, Rf = 100 kΩ from the output to the − input, + input grounded.

problems.text: Repeat Problem 19 for each circuit in Figure 12–69.
problems.how: Voltage follower: the feedback attenuation is B = 1, so Zin(VF) = (1 + Aol)·Zin and Zout(VF) = Zout/(1 + Aol) (Floyd §12–5, Eq. 12–17 and 12–18). Problem 19 asks the same for the noninverting amplifiers of Figure 12–68 (its printed answers 8.41 GΩ / 89.2 mΩ … follow the same formula).
assume: An exact KCL solution of the op-amp model agrees with the formulas to better than 0.1 %.
problems.circuit: Figure 12–69 (p.659): three voltage followers (output connected to the − input, signal on the + input). (a) Aol = 220,000, Zin = 6 MΩ, Zout = 100 Ω; (b) Aol = 100,000, Zin = 5 MΩ, Zout = 60 Ω; (c) Aol = 50,000, Zin = 800 kΩ, Zout = 75 Ω.

problems.text: A voltage-follower is driven by a voltage source with a source resistance of 75 Ω. (a) What value of compensating resistor is required for bias current, and where should the resistor be placed? (b) If the two input currents after compensation are 42 μA and 40 μA, what is the output error voltage?
answer: 75.0 Ω, in the feedback path (between the output and the inverting input)
problems.how: Bias-current compensation (Floyd §12–6): the resistor equals the resistance seen by the other input; the error is IOS × R.
assume: The two currents (42 μA and 40 μA) are the input currents after compensation: the error is the offset current × 75 Ω.

problems.text: A particular op-amp voltage-follower has an input offset voltage of 2 nV. What is the output error voltage?
problems.how: A voltage follower has unity gain, so the input offset voltage appears unchanged at the output.

problems.text: The midrange open-loop gain of a certain op-amp is 120 dB. Negative feedback reduces this gain by 50 dB. What is the closed-loop gain?
problems.how: Gains in dB subtract: 120 dB − 50 dB.

problems.text: An RC lag circuit has a critical frequency of 5 kHz. If the resistance value is 1.0 kΩ, what is XC when f = 3 kHz?
problems.how: RC lag circuit: XC = R at f = fc, and XC ∝ 1/f.

problems.text: The midrange open-loop gain of a certain op-amp is 80,000. If the open-loop critical frequency is 1 kHz, what is the open-loop gain at each of the following frequencies? (a) 100 Hz (b) 1 kHz (c) 10 kHz (d) 1 MHz
problems.how: Aol = Aol(mid)/√(1 + (f/fc(ol))²).

problems.text: An RC lag circuit has a critical frequency of 8.5 kHz. Determine the phase shift for each frequency and plot a graph of its phase angle versus frequency. (a) 100 Hz (b) 400 Hz (c) 850 Hz (d) 8.5 kHz (e) 25 kHz (f) 85 kHz
problems.how: θ = −tan⁻¹(f/fc) with fc = 8.5 kHz; plot θ against f on a log axis.

problems.text: A certain amplifier has an open-loop gain in midrange of 180,000 and an open-loop critical frequency of 1500 Hz. If the attenuation of the feedback path is 0.015, what is the closed-loop bandwidth?
problems.how: BWcl = fc(ol)(1 + B·Aol(mid)).

problems.text: Determine the effect on the output if the circuit in Figure 12–75 has the following fault (one fault at a time). (a) Output pin is shorted to the inverting input. (b) R3 is open. (c) R3 is 10 kΩ instead of 910 Ω. (d) R1 and R2 are swapped.
answer: (a) output pin shorted to the − input
Vout ≈ 0 V (≈ 37.0 nV for Vin = 100 mV, Aol = 200,000, Zout = 75 Ω): the op-amp holds the − input at the + input voltage (0 V) and sinks the source current Vin/R1 = 0.1 mA; no signal at the output
The + input has no dc path: its bias current charges the stray capacitance until the output drives into saturation at one supply rail; the ac gain (−10) is not available
Gain unchanged (−10); a dc offset appears: Vout(dc) = Ib·[R2 − R3(1 + R2/R1)] = -8.0 mV for Ib = 80 nA (instead of -0.8 μV with 910 Ω)
Gain becomes −R2/R1 = −1.0 kΩ/10 kΩ = -0.1 instead of -10.0: the output is 100 times smaller (still inverted); 100 mV in gives -10.0 mV
problems.how: Inverting amplifier with bias compensation (R3 ≈ R1 ‖ R2 = 909 Ω). Effects obtained from the ideal gain −R2/R1 and from the dc error of the input bias current, Vout(dc) = Ib·[R2 − R3(1 + R2/R1)] (exact nodal solution used as check).
assume: Ib = 80 nA is the typical LM741 value of Figure 12–77 (an assumption: the statement gives no op-amp); both inputs are taken to draw the same bias current.
The statement gives no input signal for this problem; Problem 41 uses 100 mV, which is used here only for the numbers of (a) and (d).
problems.circuit: Figure 12–75 (p.662): inverting amplifier, R1 = 1.0 kΩ from the input to the − input, R2 = 10 kΩ from the output to the − input, R3 = 910 Ω from the + input to ground (bias-current compensation).

problems.text: Refer to the partial datasheet in Figure 12–77. Determine the input impedances of a LM741 op-amp connected as an inverting amplifier with a closed-loop voltage gain of 100 and Rf = 100 kΩ.
problems.how: Inverting amplifier: Ri = Rf/|Acl| = 1.0 kΩ and Zin(I) ≈ Ri (Floyd §12–5). The LM741 typical input resistance (2.0 MΩ, datasheet Figure 12–77) only matters for the noninverting configuration, where Zin(NI) = (1 + Aol·B)·Zin.
assume: Exact KCL solution with Aol = 200,000 and Zin = 2 MΩ gives 1.001 kΩ, i.e. Ri to 0.1 %.
The statement says “input impedances” (plural); the only input impedance of the inverting amplifier is Zin(I) ≈ Ri.
problems.circuit: Figure 12–77 (p.664): partial LM741 datasheet, “LM741” column, typical values: input resistance 2.0 MΩ, large-signal voltage gain 200 V/mV (200,000), slew rate 0.5 V/μs, input bias current 80 nA.

Related Problem được kèm đề của Example mà nó dựa vào. Thời gian là giả định (6 phút mỗi bài).
note.en: Floyd Examples, Related Problems, Section Checkups and even-numbered Problems, and Jaeger Examples: the book prints no answer for these (Floyd's Related Problem answers are on the publisher's website). The answers were computed by this site with the book's own formulas and re-checked by an independent route; for the Examples the result is also compared with the worked solution printed in the book. A Related Problem is shown with the statement of the Example it builds on. The time limit is an assumption (6 minutes per exercise).

problems.text: Refer to Figure 12–77. How long does it typically take the output voltage of an LM741 to make a transition from −8 V to +8 V in response to a step input?
answer: Time for a −8 V → +8 V step at the slew rate
problems.how: Slew rate = ΔVout/Δt, so Δt = 16 V/(0.5 V/μs) = 32 μs (typical LM741 slew rate, Figure 12–77, unity gain).
assume: Slew-rate limited transition; the rise time of the small-signal response (0.3 μs typ) is much shorter.
problems.circuit: Figure 12–77 (p.664): partial LM741 datasheet; LM741 column, typical slew rate 0.5 V/μs (TA = 25 °C, unity gain).

problems.text: Design an inverting amplifier using a 741 op-amp. The voltage gain must be 68 ± 5% and the input impedance must be approximately 10 kΩ. Include bias current compensation.
answer: Compensating resistor Rc = Ri‖Rf at the + input
problems.how: Inverting amplifier: |Av| = Rf/Ri, Zin ≈ Ri (Floyd §12–4); bias compensation Rc = Ri‖Rf (§12–6).
assume: One valid design (several are possible): the book's even-numbered problems have no printed answer.
Aol of the 741 taken as 200,000 for the check.

problems.text: What is the maximum closed-loop voltage gain that can be achieved with a 741 op-amp if the bandwidth must be no less than 5 kHz?
problems.how: Gain × bandwidth = fT: with BW ≥ 5 kHz the closed-loop gain cannot exceed fT/5 kHz.
assume: 741 unity-gain bandwidth fT = 1 MHz (typical datasheet value; the book's datasheet figure is an image).

problems.text: Calculate the voltage gain for an amplifier with the following parameters: A = 100, Rid = 100 kΩ, and Ro = 100 Ω, with RI = 10 kΩ and RL = 1000 Ω. Express the result in dB.
problems.how: Voltage gain of the differential amplifier model including the source resistance RI and the load RL (Jaeger Eq. 10.33).

problems.text: Design an inverting amplifier (i.e., choose the values of R1 and R2) to have an input resistance of 20 kΩ and a gain of 40 dB.
problems.how: Ideal inverting amplifier: Rin = R1, Av = −R2/R1.
assume: Ideal op amp.

problems.text: A noninverting amplifier is designed to have a gain of 200 (46 dB) and is built using an operational amplifier with an open-loop gain of 80 dB. Find the values of the ideal gain, the actual gain, and the gain error. Express the gain error in percent.
problems.how: Finite open-loop gain: Av = Aideal·T/(1 + T), FGE = 1/(1 + T) (Jaeger §11.2).
assume: The op amp is ideal except for its finite open-loop gain A = 10,000 (80 dB).

problems.text: A noninverting amplifier is constructed with R1 = 1 kΩ and R2 = 39 kΩ using an operational amplifier with an open-loop gain of 80 dB and an output resistance of 50 Ω. Find the output resistance of the noninverting amplifier.
problems.how: Output resistance of the noninverting amplifier (Jaeger Eq. 11.25).
assume: The op amp is ideal except for finite A and nonzero Ro.
The book prints 0.198 Ω after “0.199 Ω ‖ 40 kΩ”; 50/251 = 0.1992 and the 40 kΩ in parallel changes nothing visible, so 0.199 Ω is the value (the book's last digit is a small arithmetic slip).

problems.text: Design a noninverting amplifier to have a gain of 35 dB and an output resistance of no more than 0.2 Ω. The only op amp available has an output resistance of 250 Ω. What is the minimum open-loop gain of the op amp that will meet the design requirements?
problems.how: Rout = Ro/(1 + Aβ) ≤ 0.2 Ω (Jaeger Eq. 11.26).
assume: The book rounds A to 7.03 × 10⁴ using 56.2; the exact value is 7.02 × 10⁴.

problems.text: Calculate the gain error for a voltage follower that is built using an op amp with an open-loop gain of 80 dB and a CMRR of 60 dB.
problems.how: Voltage-follower gain error with finite gain and finite CMRR (Jaeger Eq. 12.38).
assume: CMRR = 60 dB = 1000.

problems.text: An op amp has a dc gain of 100 dB and a unity-gain frequency of 10 MHz. (a) What is the bandwidth of the op amp? (b) If the op amp is used to build a noninverting amplifier with a closedloop gain of 60 dB, what is the bandwidth of the feedback amplifier? (c) Write an expression for the transfer function of the op amp. (d) Write an expression for the transfer function of the noninverting amplifier.
problems.how: Single-pole op amp: Av(s) = Ao·ωB/(s + ωB) with ωB = 2π·fT/Ao; closed loop: pole moves to ωB(1 + Ao·β).

problems.text: Anopamphasadcgainof200,000andaunity-gainfrequencyof500kHz.(a)Whatisthecutofffrequency of the op amp? (b) If the op amp is used to build an inverting amplifier with a closed-loop gain of 40 dB, what is the bandwidth of the feedback amplifier? (c) Write an expression for the transfer function of the op amp. (d) Write an expression for the transfer function of the inverting amplifier.

problems.text: The input signal in Figure 13–3(a) is applied to the comparator in Figure 13–3(b). Draw the output showing its proper relationship to the input signal. Assume the maximum output levels of the comparator are ±14 V.
answer: Reference voltage VREF = R2/(R1 + R2)·(+15 V)
+14.0 V whenever Vin > 1.63 V and −14.0 V whenever Vin < 1.63 V: a rectangular wave that is high for 39.4 % of each cycle of the ±5 V sine (switching at 19.0° and 161.0°)
problems.how: Zero-level detector shifted by the divider reference (Floyd §13–1); the output switches between the saturated levels ±14 V each time Vin crosses VREF. The book prints VREF = 1.63 V and draws the output in Figure 13–4.
assume: The duty cycle (39 %) is derived here; the book only draws the waveform.
problems.circuit: Figure 13–3 (p.670): (a) a sine wave Vin of 5 V peak (−5 V to +5 V); (b) an op-amp comparator with Vin on the + input and the reference on the − input, taken from a divider between +15 V and ground: R1 = 8.2 kΩ (from +15 V) and R2 = 1.0 kΩ (to ground).

problems.text: Determine the upper and lower trigger points for the comparator circuit in Figure 13–9. Assume that +Vout(max) = +5 V and − Vout(max) = −5 V.
problems.how: Floyd Eq. 13–1/13–2; swept the input up and down in a state machine to find the switching points (independent check).
problems.circuit: Figure 13–9 (p.673): comparator with positive feedback (Floyd Fig. 13–7 arrangement): Vin on the − input, R1 from the output to the + input, R2 from the + input to ground; in Example 13–2 R1 = R2 = 100 kΩ.

problems.text: Determine the binary number sequence of the three-digit simultaneous ADC in Figure 13–16 for the input signal in Figure 13–17 and the sampling pulses (encoder enable) shown. Draw the resulting digital output waveforms.
answer: Comparator references (R-ladder, 8 equal resistors, VREF = 8 V)
Binary output sequence (D2 D1 D0) for the 12 samples
problems.how: A flash ADC with a ladder of 8 equal resistors: comparator k switches on when Vin exceeds k·VREF/8; the priority encoder outputs the number of the highest comparator that is on, i.e. floor(Vin/LSB). With VREF = 8 V the LSB is 1 V.
assume: The 12 sample values (3.7, 5.2, 6.2, 6.6, 4.7, 1.7, 0.6, 1.0, 2.7, 5.0, 6.6, 7.2 V) are read from the dots of Figure 13–17 to about ±0.1 V; samples 8 and 10 lie on a comparator threshold, where the book's code (001 and 101) is used.
VREF = 8 V is implied by the 0–8 V axis of Figure 13–17 and the printed codes (not stated in the example).
problems.circuit: Figures 13–16 and 13–17 (pp.677–678): a three-digit simultaneous (flash) ADC: a resistor ladder of 8 equal resistors R from VREF to ground gives 7 reference voltages to 7 op-amp comparators (Vin on the + inputs); a priority encoder (inputs 1–7, enable input) outputs D2D1D0. Vin is an analog waveform between 0 and 8 V sampled by 12 enable pulses.

problems.text: Determine the output voltage of the DAC in Figure 13–27(a). The sequence of fourdigit binary codes represented by the waveforms in Figure 13–27(b) are applied to the inputs. A high level is a binary 1, and a low level is a binary 0. The least significant binary digit is D0.
answer: Contribution of each bit (D0, D1, D2, D3) = −Rf·5 V/Rk
a staircase from 0 V to -3.75 V in steps of -0.25 V
problems.how: Binary-weighted scaling adder: the − input is a virtual ground, so each 1 sends 5 V/Rk through Rf (Floyd §13–2). The book prints −0.25, −0.5, −1, −2 V per bit and the 0 to −3.75 V staircase (Figure 13–28).
assume: All 16 codes were also solved by KCL with a finite open-loop gain.
problems.circuit: Figure 13–27 (p.684): four-digit binary-weighted DAC (scaling adder): input resistors D0 = 200 kΩ, D1 = 100 kΩ, D2 = 50 kΩ, D3 = 25 kΩ to the − input, Rf = 10 kΩ, + input grounded; a binary 1 is +5 V and a 0 is 0 V. The input waveforms D0…D3 form the straight binary count 0000 to 1111.

problems.text: (a) Determine the rate of change of the output voltage in response to the input square wave, as shown for the ideal integrator in Figure 13–35(a). The output voltage is initially zero. The pulse width is 100 μs. (b) Describe the output and draw the waveform.
answer: Rate of change of Vout, Vin = +2.5 V
a triangular wave between 0 V and −5 V (5 V peak-to-peak): a falling ramp while the input is +2.5 V and a rising ramp while it is −2.5 V; ΔVout = 25 mV/μs × 200 μs = 5 V
problems.how: Ideal integrator: ΔVout/Δt = −Vin/(Ri·C) = −2.5 V/(10 kΩ × 0.01 μF) = −25 mV/μs (Floyd §13–3).
assume: BOOK INCONSISTENCY: the statement says “the pulse width is 100 μs”, but Figure 13–35(b) and the printed solution use 200 μs per half-period (ΔVout = 25 mV/μs × 200 μs = 5 V). With literally 100 μs the output would swing only 2.5 V.
problems.circuit: Figure 13–35 (p.690): ideal integrator, Ri = 10 kΩ from the input to the − input, C = 0.01 μF from the output to the − input, + input grounded. Vin is a square wave between −2.5 V and +2.5 V; in the drawing each half-period is 200 μs.

problems.text: Determine the reference voltage in Figure 13–3 if R1 = 22 kΩ and R2 = 3.3 kΩ.
problems.ctx: Example 13–1: The input signal in Figure 13–3(a) is applied to the comparator in Figure 13–3(b). Draw the output showing its proper relationship to the input signal. Assume the maximum output levels of the comparator are ±14 V.
answer: Reference voltage VREF = R2/(R1 + R2)·(+15 V)
problems.how: Same divider as Figure 13–3(b) with R1 = 22 kΩ and R2 = 3.3 kΩ.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.13 Related Problem of Example 13–1, p.670 (PDF 688)
problems.circuit: Figure 13–3 (p.670): (a) a sine wave Vin of 5 V peak (−5 V to +5 V); (b) an op-amp comparator with Vin on the + input and the reference on the − input, taken from a divider between +15 V and ground: R1 = 8.2 kΩ (from +15 V) and R2 = 1.0 kΩ (to ground).

problems.text: Determine the upper and lower trigger points in Figure 13–9 for R1 = 68 kΩ and R2 = 82 kΩ. Also assume the maximum output voltage levels are now ±7 V.

problems.how: Same circuit as Figure 13–9 with R1 = 68 kΩ, R2 = 82 kΩ and ±7 V output levels.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.13 Related Problem of Example 13–2, p.673 (PDF 691)
problems.circuit: Figure 13–9 (p.673): comparator with positive feedback (Floyd Fig. 13–7 arrangement): Vin on the − input, R1 from the output to the + input, R2 from the + input to ground; in Example 13–2 R1 = R2 = 100 kΩ.

problems.text: Determine the upper and lower trigger points for Figure 13–13 if R1 = 150 kΩ, R2 = 68 kΩ, and the zener diodes are 3.3 V devices.
problems.ctx: Example 13–3: Determine the output voltage waveform for Figure 13–13.
answer: Voltage across the zener pair Vb = VZ + 0.7 V
problems.how: Example 13–3 method: the − input stands at Vout ∓ Vb and equals the + input voltage, so Vout − Vb = Vout·R2/(R1 + R2); hence Vout = Vb(R1 + R2)/R1 and VUTP = Vb·R2/R1. The same formulas give the book's ±7.94 V and ±2.54 V for 4.7 V zeners, 100 kΩ and 47 kΩ.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.13 Related Problem of Example 13–3, p.676 (PDF 694)
problems.circuit: Figure 13–13 (p.675): comparator with hysteresis and zener bounding: Vin (a ±5 V sine) through Ri to the − input; D1 and D2, two zener diodes in series (4.7 V each in the book example), between the − input and the output; R1 = 100 kΩ from the output to the + input and R2 = 47 kΩ from the + input to ground. One zener is always forward biased (0.7 V) while the other is in breakdown.

problems.text: If a fourth input of −0.5 V is added to Figure 13–22 with a 10 kΩ resistor, what is the output voltage?
problems.ctx: Example 13–5: Determine the output voltage in Figure 13–22.
problems.how: All input resistors and Rf are 10 kΩ, so the gain is −1 for every input and the output is the inverted sum: −(3 + 1 + 8 − 0.5) V.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.13 Related Problem of Example 13–5, p.680 (PDF 698)
problems.circuit: Figure 13–22 (p.680): inverting summing amplifier, three inputs VIN1 = +3 V, VIN2 = +1 V, VIN3 = +8 V, each through 10 kΩ to the − input, Rf = 10 kΩ, + input grounded. Book result −12 V.

problems.text: Determine the output voltage in Figure 13–23 if the two input resistors are 2.2 kΩ and the feedback resistor is 18 kΩ.
problems.ctx: Example 13–6: Determine the output voltage for the summing amplifier in Figure 13–23.
problems.how: Figure 13–23 with VIN1 = 0.2 V and VIN2 = 0.5 V; R1 = R2 = 2.2 kΩ, Rf = 18 kΩ.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.13 Related Problem of Example 13–6, p.681 (PDF 699)
problems.circuit: Figure 13–23 (p.681): summing amplifier with VIN1 = 0.2 V and VIN2 = 0.5 V through R1 = R2 = 1.0 kΩ to the − input, Rf = 10 kΩ, + input grounded (book result −7 V).

problems.text: Determine the weight of each input voltage in Figure 13–25 if R1 = 22 kΩ, R2 = 82 kΩ, R3 = 56 kΩ, and Rf = 10 kΩ. Also find VOUT.
problems.ctx: Example 13–8: Determine the weight of each input voltage for the scaling adder in Figure 13–25 and find the output voltage.
problems.how: Scaling adder: the weight of each input is Rf/Rk; the inputs of Example 13–8 are +3 V, +2 V and +8 V (Figure 13–25).
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.13 Related Problem of Example 13–8, p.683 (PDF 701)
problems.circuit: Figure 13–25 (p.683): scaling adder, VIN1 = +3 V through R1, VIN2 = +2 V through R2, VIN3 = +8 V through R3, Rf = 10 kΩ; in Example 13–8 R1 = 47 kΩ, R2 = 100 kΩ, R3 = 10 kΩ (VOUT = −8.84 V).

problems.text: If the 200 kΩ resistor in Figure 13–27(a) is changed to 400 kΩ, would the other resistor values have to be changed? If so, specify the values.
problems.ctx: Example 13–9: Determine the output voltage of the DAC in Figure 13–27(a). The sequence of fourdigit binary codes represented by the waveforms in Figure 13–27(b) are applied to the inputs. A high level is a binary 1, and a low level is a binary 0. The least significant binary digit is D0.
answer: Do the other resistors have to change?
Yes. Binary weighting needs R(D0) : R(D1) : R(D2) : R(D3) = 8 : 4 : 2 : 1, so with 400 kΩ for D0 the others must be 200 kΩ, 100 kΩ and 50 kΩ (all doubled)
Effect of changing only D0 to 400 kΩ
D0 would count 1/4 as much as D1 instead of 1/2: code 0001 → -0.125 V, 0010 → -0.5 V, 0011 → -0.625 V: the staircase is no longer uniform
Output step after doubling all four input resistors (Rf = 10 kΩ)
−0.125 V per count (0 to −1.875 V); Rf = 20 kΩ restores −0.25 V per count (0 to −3.75 V)
problems.how: The weight of an input is Rf/Rk; for a binary DAC the weights must be in the ratio 1 : 2 : 4 : 8, so all the input resistors scale together (Floyd §13–2).
assume: The statement does not say whether the original output step (−0.25 V) must be kept; both options are given.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.13 Related Problem of Example 13–9, p.685 (PDF 703)
problems.circuit: Figure 13–27 (p.684): four-digit binary-weighted DAC (scaling adder): input resistors D0 = 200 kΩ, D1 = 100 kΩ, D2 = 50 kΩ, D3 = 25 kΩ to the − input, Rf = 10 kΩ, + input grounded; a binary 1 is +5 V and a 0 is 0 V. The input waveforms D0…D3 form the straight binary count 0000 to 1111.

problems.text: Modify the integrator in Figure 13–35 to make the output change from 0 to −5 V in 100 μs with the same input.
problems.ctx: Example 13–10: (a) Determine the rate of change of the output voltage in response to the input square wave, as shown for the ideal integrator in Figure 13–35(a). The output voltage is initially zero. The pulse width is 100 μs. (b) Describe the output and draw the waveform.
answer: C for 0 → −5 V in 100 μs with Ri = 10 kΩ, Vin = 2.5 V
problems.how: The slope must be 5 V/100 μs = 50 mV/μs = Vin/(Ri·C), so Ri·C = 2.5 V/(50 mV/μs) = 50 μs: halve the time constant (C = 5 nF with Ri = 10 kΩ, or Ri = 5 kΩ with C = 0.01 μF).
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.13 Related Problem of Example 13–10, p.690 (PDF 708)
problems.circuit: Figure 13–35 (p.690): ideal integrator, Ri = 10 kΩ from the input to the − input, C = 0.01 μF from the output to the − input, + input grounded. Vin is a square wave between −2.5 V and +2.5 V; in the drawing each half-period is 200 μs.

problems.text: What would the output voltage be if the feedback resistor in Figure 13–40 is changed to 3.3 kΩ?
problems.ctx: Example 13–11: Determine the output voltage of the ideal op-amp differentiator in Figure 13–40 for the triangular-wave input shown.
answer: Vout during the rising ramp / falling ramp
problems.how: Differentiator: Vout = −Rf·C·(ΔVin/Δt) = −(3.3 μs)(2 V/μs) = −6.6 V on the rising ramp (the book gets −4.4 V for Rf = 2.2 kΩ).
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.13 Related Problem of Example 13–11, p.693 (PDF 711)
problems.circuit: Figure 13–40 (p.692): ideal op-amp differentiator, C = 0.001 μF in series with the input to the − input, Rf = 2.2 kΩ from the output to the − input, + input grounded. Vin is a triangular wave between −5 V and +5 V, 5 μs per ramp (10 μs period).

problems.text: In Figure 13–47, R5 = 47 kΩ. What is the output voltage if R1 opens?
problems.ctx: Example 13–13: (a) What is the normal output voltage in Figure 13–47? (b) What is the output voltage if R2 opens? (c) What happens if R5 opens?
problems.how: With R1 open the 1 V input is disconnected; the remaining inputs are amplified by −Rf/R = −47 kΩ/10 kΩ = −4.7.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.13 Related Problem of Example 13–13, p.697 (PDF 715)
problems.circuit: Figure 13–47 (p.697): summing amplifier, four inputs VIN1 = 1 V, VIN2 = 0.5 V, VIN3 = 0.2 V, VIN4 = 0.1 V, each through 10 kΩ (R1…R4) to the − input, feedback R5 = 10 kΩ in the book example (−1.8 V).

problems.text: A certain scaling adder has two inputs, one having twice the weight of the other. If the resistor value for the lower-weighted input is 10 kΩ, what is the value of the other input resistor?
problems.how: In a scaling adder the weight of an input is Rf/Rk, so twice the weight needs half the resistance: 10 kΩ/2.
assume: The lower-weighted input has the larger resistor (10 kΩ).

problems.text: If VIN2 is changed to −1 V in Figure 13–22, the output voltage will (a) increase (b) decrease (c) not change
problems.how: VOUT = −(VIN1 + VIN2 + VIN3): VIN2 falls from +1 V to −1 V, the sum falls from 12 V to 10 V and VOUT rises from −12 V to −10 V.
problems.circuit: Figure 13–22 (p.680): inverting summing amplifier, VIN1 = +3 V, VIN2 = +1 V, VIN3 = +8 V, three 10 kΩ input resistors, Rf = 10 kΩ.

problems.text: If VIN3 is changed to −7 V in Figure 13–24, the output voltage will (a) increase (b) decrease (c) not change
problems.how: Averaging amplifier, Rf/R = 1/4: VOUT = −(1/4)(VIN1 + VIN2 + VIN3 + VIN4); the sum drops from 10 V to 0 V, so VOUT goes from −2.5 V to 0 V.
problems.circuit: Figure 13–24 (p.682): averaging amplifier, four inputs VIN1…VIN4 = +1, +2, +3, +4 V each through 100 kΩ to the − input, Rf = 25 kΩ, + input grounded (book result −2.5 V).

problems.text: The waveforms given in Figure 13–71(a) are observed at the indicated points in Figure 13–71(b). Is the circuit operating properly? If not, what is a likely fault?
answer: Healthy circuit (zener pair drop Vb = 4.3 + 0.7 = 5.0 V)
Vout = ±10.0 V, VC = ±5.0 V: it should switch between +10 V and −10 V with trigger points ±5 V
VB = +10 V / −1.4 V and VC = +5 V / −0.7 V: the positive half is correct, the negative half is not

One of the zener diodes is shorted (the one that should be in breakdown when the output is negative): the negative output is then limited by a single 0.7 V junction, giving Vb = 0.7 V, Vout = −2·0.7 = -1.4 V and VC = −0.7 V, exactly the observed values
problems.how: Zener-bounded comparator with hysteresis (Example 13–3): Vout = ±Vb(R1 + R2)/R1 and VUTP/VLTP = ±Vb·R2/R1 with Vb = VZ + 0.7 V. The observed negative levels fit Vb = 0.7 V, i.e. one zener replaced by a short.
assume: An open zener would stop the output from switching to that level at all; the observation shows a limited negative level, so a short is more consistent.
problems.circuit: Figure 13–71 (p.715): (b) a comparator with hysteresis and zener bounding (Figure 13–13 type): input A through Ri = 100 kΩ to the − input, two 4.3 V zeners D1 and D2 in series between the − input (node) and the output B, R1 = 10 kΩ from B to the + input (node C) and R2 = 10 kΩ from C to ground. (a) the observed waveforms: VA a ±6 V sine; VB switches between +10 V and −1.4 V; VC between +5 V and −0.7 V; the output switches high when VA falls to −0.7 V and low when VA reaches +5 V.

problems.text: Assume that a 1.0 kΩ resistor is inadvertently used for R1 in Figure 13–50. What effect does this have on the circuit operation?
answer: Reference range with R1 = R3 = 56 kΩ (as drawn)
Effect on the duty cycle (10 V peak sine)

minimum 0 % (the reference exceeds the 10 V peak, so over the top 9.08 % of the potentiometer travel the output never goes high), maximum 90.8 % instead of 93.7 %: the range is no longer symmetrical and part of the control is wasted
problems.how: Reference voltage = +12 V − I·(R1 + x·R2) with I = 24 V/(R1 + R2 + R3); the pulse is high while the sine exceeds the reference, duty = (π − 2·asin(Vref/Vp))/(2π). The 10 V peak sine of Problem 27 is used (Application Activity text).
assume: The effect is derived here (the book gives no answer for this even-numbered problem); the duty cycles are computed by sampling the sine wave.
problems.circuit: Figure 13–50 (p.700): sine/pulse generator: a 10 V peak sine wave goes to the + input of an LM111 comparator; the − input is the wiper of a 500 kΩ potentiometer R2 between R1 = 56 kΩ (to +12 V) and R3 = 56 kΩ (to −12 V); output pulled up to +5 V by R4 = 1 kΩ.

problems.text: Redesign the circuit in Figure 13–50 for a 5 V peak sine wave.
answer: Required reference range (same 98 % of the sine peak as the original)
R1 = R3 for that range (R2 = 500 kΩ, ±12 V supplies)
362.0 kΩ (standard value 360 kΩ gives ±4.92 V and a duty-cycle range of 5.77 % … 94.2 %)
problems.how: The reference at the ends of the potentiometer is ±(12 V − I·R1) with I = 24 V/(2R1 + R2). The original design (R1 = 56 kΩ) gives ±9.8 V for a 10 V peak sine (duty 6.4 %–93.6 %); for a 5 V peak sine the same fractions need ±4.9 V.
assume: A design problem: the book prints no answer. Assumed: the pot R2 = 500 kΩ and the ±12 V supplies stay, only R1 = R3 change, and the duty range of the original design is kept (the pulse spec of Table 13–1 is 15 %–85 %, which any R1 above this value also meets).
Another valid design would change R2 or the supply instead.
problems.circuit: Figure 13–50 (p.700): sine/pulse generator: 10 V peak sine on the + input of an LM111; − input from the wiper of a 500 kΩ potentiometer R2 between R1 = 56 kΩ (to +12 V) and R3 = 56 kΩ (to −12 V); R4 = 1 kΩ pull-up to +5 V.

problems.text: Design an inverting amplifier (i.e., choose the values of R1 and R2) to have an input resistance of 20 kΩ and a gain of 40 dB.
problems.how: Ideal inverting amplifier: Rin = R1, Av = −R2/R1.
assume: Ideal op amp.

problems.text: Find the magnitude and phase of this voltage transfer function for ω = 0 and ω = 3 rad/s.
problems.ctx: Transfer function of the example: Av(s) = 50(s² + 4)/(s² + 2s + 2).
problems.how: Substitute s = jω and take magnitude and phase of the complex number.

problems.text: Design an active low-pass filter (choose the values of R1, R2, andC) with fH = 2 kHz, Rin = 5 kΩ, and Av = 40 dB.
answer: With standard values R1 = 5.1 kΩ, R2 = 510 kΩ, C = 160 pF
problems.how: Active low-pass filter: inverting amplifier with C in parallel with R2; Rin = R1, |Av| = R2/R1, fH = 1/(2π·R2·C).
assume: Standard values are the nearest of the Appendix A tables, as in the book.

Extra: output for the 50 μV, 75 Ω source (the source resistance only divides the input)

problems.text: Determine the efficiency of the power amplifier in Figure 7–5 (Example 7–1).
answer: Input resistance Rin(tot) = R1 ‖ R2 ‖ β(RE1 + r′e)
problems.how: Floyd Example 7–2 with the circuit of Example 7–1: Av1 = Rc1/(RE1 + r′e) = 27.9; PDC = ICC·VCC with IE(Q3) = VE(Q3)/RE3 = 8.2 V/33 Ω ≈ 0.25 A; η = Pout/PDC. Pout is also checked as Vout²/RL (Vout = Av·Vin).
assume: BOOK ERROR 1: the printed solution says 50 mV peak-to-peak is 35.4 mV rms. 35.4 mV rms is 50 mV PEAK (100 mV pp); 50 mV pp is 17.7 mV rms. The book's numbers (Pin = 149 nW, Pout = 122 mW, η ≈ 4 %) are reproduced here for 35.4 mV to confirm the circuit values, but the figure says 50 mV pp, which gives η ≈ 1 %.

BOOK ERROR 2 (also in Example 7–1): the printed Rin(tot) = 56 kΩ ‖ 10 kΩ ‖ 200(68 Ω + 14 Ω) = 8.4 kΩ is only 56 kΩ ‖ 10 kΩ; with the 16.4 kΩ branch it is 5.6 kΩ, so the power gain of Example 7–1 is about 5.5·10⁵, not 817,330. Pout does not depend on it.

problems.how: Power taken from the supply = output power + power dissipated in the transistor; η = Pout/(Pout + PD(avg)) (Floyd §7–3).
assume: The 100 mW is the average power dissipated in the transistor.

problems.text: Refer to the class AB amplifier in Figure 7–46. (a) What is the maximum power that could be delivered to the load resistor? (b) Assume the power supply voltage is raised to 24 V. What is the new maximum power that could be delivered to the load resistor?

Actual rms signal at the amplifier input

assume: r′e from the dc current 6.8 mA of Problem 15(a); ignoring r′e changes the result in the third digit.

answer: ≈ 80 kHz (the book's reading of the point where the curve begins to drop)

problems.text: The input to the OTA amplitude modulator in Figure 14–25 is a 50 mV peak-to-peak, 1 MHz sine wave. Determine the output signal, given the modulation voltage shown is applied to the bias input.
answer: a 1 MHz carrier whose amplitude follows the 1 kHz modulating sine between 1.23 V and 2.51 V (amplitude modulation)

assume: The book multiplies the 50 mV peak-to-peak input by the gain, so the quoted values are peak-to-peak amplitudes of the carrier.

New gm = K·IBIAS and Av = gm·RL
11.0 mS, Av = 110.0: yes, the gain increases from 80.5 to about 110.0

problems.text: A certain band-pass filter has a center frequency of 15 kHz and a bandwidth of 1 kHz. Determine Q and classify the filter as narrow-band or wide-band.
problems.how: Band-pass filter: Q = f0/BW; Q > 10 is narrow-band (Floyd §15–1).

problems.text: If resistor R2 in the feedback circuit of an active single-pole filter of the type in Figure 15–6 is 10 kΩ, what value must R1 be to obtain a maximally flat Butterworth response?
problems.how: Damping factor DF = 2 − R1/R2; Butterworth needs DF = 1.414, so R1/R2 = 0.586 (Floyd Table 15–1). The book prints R1 = 5.86 kΩ and picks 5.6 kΩ.
assume: The independent check uses an exact Sallen-Key response: with R1/R2 = 0.586 its gain at fc is 1/√2 of the dc gain (maximally flat).
problems.circuit: Figure 15–6 (p.770): general active single-pole (first-order) filter block: a frequency-selective RC circuit drives the + input of a noninverting op-amp whose gain and damping factor are set by the feedback resistors R1 (from the output to the − input) and R2 (from the − input to ground).

problems.text: For the four-pole filter in Figure 15–12(b), determine the capacitance values required to produce a critical frequency of 2680 Hz if all the resistors in the RC low-pass circuits are 1.8 kΩ. Also select values for the feedback resistors to get a Butterworth response.
problems.how: Both stages need the same fc, so with equal R the capacitors are equal: C = 1/(2πR·fc); the feedback ratios of Table 15–1 for a four-pole Butterworth filter are R1/R2 = 0.152 and R3/R4 = 1.235 with R2 = R4 = 1.8 kΩ.
assume: The exact response of the two cascaded sections with the book's values is 3 dB down at 2.68 kHz.
problems.circuit: Figure 15–12(b) (p.775): four-pole Sallen-Key low-pass filter made of two cascaded two-pole stages: stage 1 with RA1 = RB1 (RC low-pass circuit), CA1 = CB1 and feedback resistors R1 and R2; stage 2 with RA2 = RB2, CA2 = CB2 and feedback resistors R3 and R4.

problems.text: Choose values for the Sallen-Key high-pass filter in Figure 15–15 to implement an equal-value second-order Butterworth response with a critical frequency of approximately 10 kHz.
answer: C = CA = CB = 1/(2πR·fc) with R = RA = RB = R2 = 3.3 kΩ
If R1 = 3.3 kΩ is chosen instead
problems.how: Equal-value Sallen-Key high-pass: fc = 1/(2πRC), R1/R2 = 0.586 for a Butterworth response (Floyd §15–4). The book prints 0.0048 μF and 1.93 kΩ.
assume: The exact response is 3 dB down at 9.998 kHz.
problems.circuit: Figure 15–15 (p.777): Sallen-Key high-pass filter: input through CA to a node, CB from that node to the + input, RA from the node to the output (feedback), RB from the + input to ground; gain-setting resistors R1 (output to − input) and R2 (− input to ground).

problems.text: Verify that the band-stop filter in Figure 15–26 has a center frequency of 60 Hz, and optimize the filter for a Q of 10.
answer: R5 for Q = 10 with R6 = 3.3 kΩ: R5 = (3Q − 1)·R6
problems.how: The band-stop filter uses the state-variable filter: f0 equals the critical frequency of the integrators and Q = (1/3)(R5/R6 + 1), so R5 = (3Q − 1)R6 (Floyd §15–6). R6 is free to choose.
assume: Exact solution of the whole circuit (state-variable filter + summing amplifier): notch at 60.29 Hz, depth > 60 dB, Q = 10.0.
problems.circuit: Figure 15–26 (p.786): band-stop (notch) filter made from a state-variable filter and a summing amplifier: R1 = R2 = R3 = 10 kΩ, integrators R4 = R7 = 12 kΩ with C1 = C2 = 0.22 μF, Q-setting resistors R5 (from the BP output) and R6 (to ground); the high-pass and low-pass outputs are added by R8 = R9 = R10 = 10 kΩ.

problems.text: What is the damping factor for R2 = 10 kΩ and R1 = 5.6 kΩ?
problems.ctx: Example 15–2: If resistor R2 in the feedback circuit of an active single-pole filter of the type in Figure 15–6 is 10 kΩ, what value must R1 be to obtain a maximally flat Butterworth response?
problems.how: Damping factor of the two-pole Sallen-Key filter: DF = 2 − R1/R2 (Floyd §15–2).
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.15 Related Problem of Example 15–2, p.771 (PDF 789)

problems.text: Determine fc for Figure 15–11 if RA = RB = R2 = 2.2 kΩ and CA = CB = 0.01 μF. Also determine the value of R1 for a Butterworth response.
problems.ctx: Example 15–3: Determine the critical frequency of the Sallen-Key low-pass filter in Figure 15–11, and set the value of R1 for an approximate Butterworth response.
problems.how: Equal-value Sallen-Key: fc = 1/(2πRC) with RA = RB = 2.2 kΩ and CA = CB = 0.01 μF; R1/R2 = 0.586 for DF = 1.414 (Example 15–3 method).
assume: The exact response with R1 = 0.586·R2 is 3 dB down at 7.235 kHz.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.15 Related Problem of Example 15–3, p.774 (PDF 792)
problems.circuit: Figure 15–11 (p.774): Sallen-Key low-pass filter: input through RA to a node, RB from that node to the + input, CA from the node to the output (feedback), CB from the + input to ground; gain-setting resistors R1 (output to − input) and R2 (− input to ground). In Example 15–3 RA = RB = R2 = 1.0 kΩ and CA = CB = 0.022 μF (fc = 7.23 kHz, R1 = 586 Ω).

problems.ctx: Example 15–6: Determine the center frequency, maximum gain, and bandwidth for the filter in Figure 15–19.
problems.how: Multiple-feedback band-pass (Floyd §15–5): f0 = (1/2πC)·√((R1 + R3)/(R1R2R3)), A0 = R2/2R1, Q = π·f0·C·R2, BW = f0/Q; Example 15–6 (R2 = 180 kΩ) gives 736 Hz, 1.32 and 177 Hz.

problems.text: How would you change the center frequency to 120 Hz in Figure 15–26?
problems.ctx: Example 15–8: Verify that the band-stop filter in Figure 15–26 has a center frequency of 60 Hz, and optimize the filter for a Q of 10.
answer: 6.03 kΩ (standard 6.2 kΩ gives 116.7 Hz; 6.0 kΩ gives 120.6 Hz)
Or keep R4 = R7 = 12 kΩ and change C1 = C2
problems.how: f0 = 1/(2πRC) of the integrators is inversely proportional to R·C: doubling the centre frequency halves R4 = R7 (both, so the integrators stay matched) or halves C1 = C2; R5/R6 (the Q) need not change.
assume: Exact solution of the circuit with R4 = R7 = 6.03 kΩ: notch at 120.0 Hz.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.15 Related Problem of Example 15–8, p.786 (PDF 804)
problems.circuit: Figure 15–26 (p.786): band-stop (notch) filter made from a state-variable filter and a summing amplifier: R1 = R2 = R3 = 10 kΩ, integrators R4 = R7 = 12 kΩ with C1 = C2 = 0.22 μF, Q-setting resistors R5 (from the BP output) and R6 (to ground); the high-pass and low-pass outputs are added by R8 = R9 = R10 = 10 kΩ.

problems.text: Without changing the response curve, adjust the component values in the filter of Figure 15–45 to make it an equal-value filter. Select C = 0.22 μF for both stages.
answer: Critical frequency of each stage fc = 1/(2π·√(R1R2C1C2))
Equal-value stage with C = 0.22 μF: R = 1/(2π·fc·C)
3.81 kΩ (standard 3.9 kΩ gives fc = 185.5 Hz; 3.6 kΩ gives 201.0 Hz)

R1 = R2 = R5 = R6 = 3.8 kΩ (≈ 3.9 kΩ), C1 = C2 = C3 = C4 = 0.22 μF; the gain-setting resistors R3/R4 = 0.147 (DF = 1.853) and R7/R8 = 1.214 (DF = 0.786) are unchanged: they are the four-pole Butterworth ratios of Table 15–1 (0.152 and 1.235), so the response curve is kept
problems.how: In the book's model the response (damping factor) of an equal-value Sallen-Key stage depends only on R3/R4 (R7/R8) and fc = 1/(2πRC); the unequal-value circuit has fc = 1/(2π√(R1R2C1C2)) = 190 Hz. Replacing both resistors by R = 1/(2π·fc·C) with C = 0.22 μF keeps fc and the feedback resistors keep the Butterworth shape.
assume: Exact check of the new circuit: the cascade is 3 dB down at 187.0 Hz.

This follows the textbook equal-value model; the exact response of the original unequal-value circuit is not identical (its damping depends on the component ratios), so “without changing the response curve” is interpreted as keeping fc and the Butterworth feedback ratios.
problems.circuit: Figure 15–45 (p.805): two cascaded Sallen-Key low-pass sections, each with unequal values. Stage 1: R1 = 4.7 kΩ, R2 = 6.8 kΩ, C1 = 0.22 μF (feedback capacitor), C2 = 0.1 μF (to ground), gain resistors R3 = 1.0 kΩ and R4 = 6.8 kΩ. assume: R5 and R6 are not in the figure (they are to be chosen); only their ratio matters: R6 = 1.0 kΩ is an arbitrary choice.
Exact solution of the three-op-amp circuit gives f0 = 1.326 kHz and Q = 50.0.
