problems.text: Determine the resonant frequency for the Wien-bridge oscillator in Figure 16–12. Also, calculate the setting for Rf assuming the internal drain-source resistance, rd′ s, of the JFET is 500 Ω when oscillations are stable.
answer: Rf for a closed-loop gain of 3: Rf = (Av − 1)(R3 + r′ds)
problems.how: Wien-bridge: fr = 1/(2πRC); oscillations need a closed-loop gain of 3 to offset the lead-lag attenuation 1/3, and the amplifier is a noninverting stage with Ri = R3 + r′ds (Floyd §16–2). The book prints 1.59 kHz and 3.0 kΩ.
problems.circuit: Figure 16–12 (p.814): Wien-bridge oscillator with automatic gain control: lead-lag network R1 = R2 = 10 kΩ, C1 = C2 = 0.01 μF on the + input; negative feedback from the output to the − input through the 10 kΩ potentiometer Rf, with a JFET (2N5458, drain-source resistance r′ds) and R3 = 1.0 kΩ in the source in series to ground; diode D1 (1N914), R4 = 10 kΩ and C3 = 1.0 μF rectify the output to bias the JFET gate.

problems.text: (a) Determine the frequency for the oscillator in Figure 16–21. Assume there is negligible loading on the feedback circuit and that its Q is greater than 10. (b) Find the frequency if the oscillator is loaded to a point where the Q drops to 8.
problems.how: Colpitts oscillator: the tank capacitors C1 and C2 are in series, fr = 1/(2π√(L·CT)); a loaded tank lowers it by √(Q²/(Q² + 1)) (Floyd §16–4). The book prints 0.0091 μF, 7.46 kHz and 7.40 kHz.
assume: Exact lossy-tank solution for Q = 8: 7.406 kHz.
problems.circuit: Figure 16–21 (p.821): Colpitts oscillator, +12 V: bias resistors R1, R2, collector resistor R3, emitter resistor R4, coupling/bypass capacitors C3, C4, C5; the tank is L = 50 mH with C1 = 0.1 μF and C2 = 0.01 μF in series (the capacitive divider gives the feedback).

problems.text: Determine the frequency of oscillation of the circuit in Figure 16–30. To what value must R1 be changed to make the frequency 20 kHz?
problems.how: Triangular-wave oscillator (Floyd Eq. 16–10); the book prints 8.25 kHz and 4.13 kΩ.
assume: The simulation of the integrator + comparator confirms both frequencies.
problems.circuit: Figure 16–30 (p.827): triangular-wave oscillator with two op-amps: an integrator with R1 = 10 kΩ and C = 0.01 μF (input from the comparator output) and a comparator with hysteresis whose positive-feedback resistors are R2 = 33 kΩ and R3 = 10 kΩ; the comparator output swings between +Vmax and −Vmax. Book formulas: VUTP = +Vmax·(R3/R2), fr = (1/(4R1C))(R2/R3).

problems.text: (a) Find the amplitude and frequency of the sawtooth output in Figure 16–32. Assume that the forward PUT voltage, VF, is approximately 1 V. (b) Sketch the output waveform.
answer: Gate voltage VG = R4/(R3 + R4)·(+V) = peak of the sawtooth
a sawtooth ramping from about 1 V up to 7.5 V in 1.59 ms, then dropping back quickly when the PUT fires
problems.how: PUT sawtooth generator (Floyd §16–5): the ramp slope is |VIN|/(Ri·C) and the PUT fires when the output reaches VG. The book prints 7.5 V, 6.5 V, 628 Hz and 1.59 ms.
assume: The book neglects the loading of the 68 kΩ/10 kΩ divider by Ri (the current is taken as |VIN|/Ri); including it lowers the frequency to about 579.0 Hz.
problems.circuit: Figure 16–32 (p.828): sawtooth generator with a PUT: an op-amp integrator whose input resistor Ri = 100 kΩ is fed from a divider between −15 V: R1 = 68 kΩ (to −15 V) and R2 = 10 kΩ (to ground); feedback capacitor C = 0.0047 μF; the PUT (anode at the − input, cathode at the output through the gate network) has its gate at the divider R3 = 10 kΩ (from +15 V) and R4 = 10 kΩ (to ground), so VG = 7.5 V.

problems.text: A 555 timer configured to run in the astable mode (oscillator) is shown in Figure 16–41. Determine the frequency of the output and the duty cycle.
problems.how: 555 astable (Floyd Eq. 16–12 and 16–13). The book prints 5.64 kHz and 59.5 %.
assume: A time-stepped simulation gives 5.652 kHz and 59.5 % (the book's 1.44 is 1/0.694).
problems.circuit: Figure 16–41 (p.834): astable 555 timer on +5.5 V: R1 = 2.2 kΩ (VCC to the discharge pin), R2 = 4.7 kΩ (discharge pin to the threshold/trigger pins), Cext = 0.022 μF to ground, 0.01 μF on the control pin. Figure 16–40: a diode D1 across R2 makes Cext charge through R1 only.

problems.text: (a) If R1, R2, and R3 in Figure 16–14 are changed to 8.2 kΩ, what value must Rf be for oscillation? (b) What is the value of fr?
problems.ctx: Example 16–2: (a) Determine the value of Rf necessary for the circuit in Figure 16–14 to operate as an oscillator. (b) Determine the frequency of oscillation.
problems.how: Phase-shift oscillator: the three-section network attenuates by 29 at fr = 1/(2π√6·RC) with a phase shift of 180°, so the inverting amplifier needs Acl = 29: Rf = 29·R3 (Floyd §16–2).
assume: Exact solution of the unloaded three-section network: 180° at 7.924 kHz with attenuation 29.0.

problems.text: What is the amplitude of the triangular wave in Figure 16–30 if the comparator output is ±10 V?
problems.ctx: Example 16–4: Determine the frequency of oscillation of the circuit in Figure 16–30. To what value must R1 be changed to make the frequency 20 kHz?
answer: Peak-to-peak amplitude of the triangular wave
problems.how: The comparator trigger points set the triangle: VUTP = +Vmax(R3/R2), VLTP = −Vmax(R3/R2) (Floyd §16–5): ±10 V × 10 kΩ/33 kΩ. The frequency (8.25 kHz) does not depend on Vmax.
assume: A time-stepped simulation of the integrator and comparator gives a peak of 3.03 V and 8.24 kHz.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.16 Related Problem of Example 16–4, p.827 (PDF 845)
problems.circuit: Figure 16–30 (p.827): triangular-wave oscillator with two op-amps: an integrator with R1 = 10 kΩ and C = 0.01 μF (input from the comparator output) and a comparator with hysteresis whose positive-feedback resistors are R2 = 33 kΩ and R3 = 10 kΩ; the comparator output swings between +Vmax and −Vmax. Book formulas: VUTP = +Vmax·(R3/R2), fr = (1/(4R1C))(R2/R3).

problems.text: If Ri is changed to 56 kΩ in Figure 16–32, what is the frequency?
problems.ctx: Example 16–5: (a) Find the amplitude and frequency of the sawtooth output in Figure 16–32. Assume that the forward PUT voltage, VF, is approximately 1 V. (b) Sketch the output waveform.
answer: the slope is inversely proportional to Ri: 628 Hz × 100 kΩ/56 kΩ
problems.how: Same method as Example 16–5: VIN = −1.92 V, Vp − VF = 6.5 V, now with Ri = 56 kΩ.
assume: Including the loading of the divider by Ri (not done in the book) the frequency would be about 973.0 Hz.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.16 Related Problem of Example 16–5, p.829 (PDF 847)
problems.circuit: Figure 16–32 (p.828): sawtooth generator with a PUT: an op-amp integrator whose input resistor Ri = 100 kΩ is fed from a divider between −15 V: R1 = 68 kΩ (to −15 V) and R2 = 10 kΩ (to ground); feedback capacitor C = 0.0047 μF; the PUT (anode at the − input, cathode at the output through the gate network) has its gate at the divider R3 = 10 kΩ (from +15 V) and R4 = 10 kΩ (to ground), so VG = 7.5 V.

problems.text: Determine the duty cycle in Figure 16–41 if a diode is connected across R2 as indicated in Figure 16–40.
problems.ctx: Example 16–6: A 555 timer configured to run in the astable mode (oscillator) is shown in Figure 16–41. Determine the frequency of the output and the duty cycle.
answer: Duty cycle with the diode across R2: tH = 0.694·R1·C, tL = 0.694·R2·C
problems.how: With D1 across R2, Cext charges through R1 only and discharges through R2: duty cycle = R1/(R1 + R2) (Floyd §16–6).
assume: The diode forward drop (≈ 0.7 V) is neglected, as in the book; a time-stepped simulation confirms the duty cycle.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.16 Related Problem of Example 16–6, p.834 (PDF 852)
problems.circuit: Figure 16–41 (p.834): astable 555 timer on +5.5 V: R1 = 2.2 kΩ (VCC to the discharge pin), R2 = 4.7 kΩ (discharge pin to the threshold/trigger pins), Cext = 0.022 μF to ground, 0.01 μF on the control pin. Figure 16–40: a diode D1 across R2 makes Cext charge through R1 only.

problems.text: A certain lead-lag circuit has R1 = R2 and C1 = C2. An input voltage of 5 V rms is applied. The input frequency equals the resonant frequency of the circuit. What is the rms output voltage?
problems.how: At the resonant frequency the lead-lag network has B = 1/3 and 0° phase shift (Floyd §16–3).

problems.text: Calculate the frequency of oscillation for each circuit in Figure 16–60 and identify the type of oscillator. Assume Q > 10 in each case.
answer: Colpitts oscillator (one inductor, two capacitors C1 and C3 forming the capacitive divider)
Hartley oscillator (two inductors L1 and L2 with one capacitor C2)
problems.how: Colpitts: fr = 1/(2π√(L·CT)) with the two tank capacitors in series; Hartley: fr = 1/(2π√(LT·C)) with LT = L1 + L2 (Floyd §16–4). Q > 10 so loading is neglected.
assume: The two inductors of the Hartley circuit are taken as uncoupled (no mutual inductance is given).
The coupling and bypass capacitors (1 μF) are taken as ac shorts.
problems.circuit: Figure 16–60 (p.848): (a) a transistor oscillator whose tank is L1 = 5 mH with C1 = 100 pF (from the inductor's lower end to ground) and C3 = 1000 pF (from the collector to ground, ac), feedback taken from the C1 junction through C2 = 1 μF to the base (C4 = 1 μF bypass); (b) a transistor oscillator with L1 = 1.5 mH and L2 = 10 mH each from a side of the tank to ground and C2 = 470 pF across both (C1, C3, C4 = 1 μF coupling/bypass capacitors).

problems.text: Determine the amplitude and frequency of the output voltage in Figure 16–63. Use 1 V as the forward PUT voltage.
answer: Gate voltage VG = R5/(R4 + R5)·(+12 V) = peak of the output
Input voltage VIN = R2/(R1 + R2)·(−12 V)
problems.how: PUT sawtooth generator solved as Example 16–5: the gate divider R4 = 100 kΩ, R5 = 47 kΩ from +12 V sets the firing level VG; the input divider R1 = 100 kΩ, R2 = 22 kΩ from −12 V sets the ramp current through R3 = 100 kΩ into C = 0.0022 μF.
assume: As in the book's Example 16–5 the loading of the input divider by R3 is neglected; including it the frequency would be 2.94 kHz.
problems.circuit: Figure 16–63 (p.849): PUT sawtooth generator: an op-amp integrator with C = 0.0022 μF; the input R3 = 100 kΩ is fed from the divider R1 = 100 kΩ (to −12 V) and R2 = 22 kΩ (to ground); the PUT gate is set by R4 = 100 kΩ (from +12 V) and R5 = 47 kΩ (to ground).

problems.text: When the ac input voltage of a certain power supply changes, the input to the voltage regulator decreases by 5 V as a result, and the output of the regulator decreases by 0.25 V. The nominal output is 15 V. Determine the line regulation in %/V.
problems.how: Floyd Eq. 17–2: line regulation = (ΔVOUT/VOUT)·100 %/ΔVIN.

problems.text: A certain voltage regulator has a 12 V output when there is no load (IL = 0).When there is a full-load current of 10 mA, the output voltage is 11.9 V. Express the voltage regulation as a percentage change from no-load to full-load and also as a percentage change for each mA change in load current.
problems.how: Floyd Eq. 17–3: load regulation = (VNL − VFL)/VFL·100 %; the load current changes by 10 mA.

problems.text: In Figure 17–15, what power rating must R1 have if the maximum input voltage is 12.5 V?
answer: Worst case: output shorted, VR1 = VIN
7.1 W → use a resistor rated at least 10 W
problems.how: With the output short-circuited VOUT = 0, so VR1 = 12.5 V and PR1 = 12.5²/22 Ω = 7.10 W; choose the next standard rating, 10 W (Floyd §17–2).
problems.circuit: Figure 17–15 (p.862): series regulator with current limiting: R1 = 22 Ω in series with the input (VIN to the output), the pass transistor Q1 with R2 = 1.0 kΩ, R3 = 10 kΩ and R4 = 10 kΩ; the worst case for R1 is a short-circuited output (VOUT = 0), when all of VIN appears across R1.

problems.text: Determine the minimum and maximum output voltages for the voltage regulator in Figure 17–30. Assume IADJ = 50 μA.
answer: VOUT(max), R2 = 5 kΩ: VREF(1 + R2/R1) + IADJ·R2
problems.how: LM317 (Floyd §17–5): the regulator holds VREF = 1.25 V across R1, so the current through R1 plus IADJ flows in R2. The book prints 1.25 V and 29.9 V.
assume: The 35 V input is high enough for 29.9 V out (a dropout margin of a few volts is needed).
problems.circuit: Figure 17–30 (p.872): adjustable LM317 regulator: input +35 V; R1 = 220 Ω between the output and the adjustment terminal; R2 = 5 kΩ (maximum) potentiometer from the adjustment terminal to ground; decoupling capacitors C1, C2, C3. VOUT = VREF(1 + R2/R1) + IADJ·R2 with VREF = 1.25 V.

problems.text: What value is Rext if the maximum current to be handled internally by the voltage regulator in Figure 17–34 is set at 700 mA?
problems.how: Qext turns on when the voltage across Rext reaches its base-emitter voltage 0.7 V, which happens at Imax = 0.7 V/Rext; so Rext = 0.7 V/0.7 A = 1 Ω (Floyd §17–6). Check with the printed answer of Problem 25: 0.7 V/250 mA = 2.8 Ω.
problems.circuit: Figure 17–34 (p.876): fixed three-terminal regulator (78xx) with an external pass transistor Qext (pnp): Rext is connected between the input terminal of the regulator and the base/emitter of Qext so that Qext turns on when the current through the regulator (and Rext) makes VRext = 0.7 V; the load current is IL = Iext + Imax.

problems.text: What must be the minimum power rating for the external pass transistor used with a 7824 regulator in a circuit such as that shown in Figure 17–34? The input voltage is 30 V and the load resistance is 10 Ω. The maximum internal current is to be 700 mA. Assume that there is no heat sink for this calculation. Keep in mind that the use of a heat sink increases the effective power rating of the transistor and you can use a lower rated transistor.
answer: Current through Qext: Iext = IL − Imax
10.2 W → choose a transistor rated at least 15 W
problems.how: External pass transistor (Floyd §17–6): the regulator handles Imax = 0.7 A and Qext the rest of the load current, dropping VIN − VOUT = 6 V. The book prints 2.4 A, 1.7 A and 10.2 W.
assume: No heat sink is assumed, as stated.
problems.circuit: Figure 17–34 (p.876): fixed three-terminal regulator (78xx) with an external pass transistor Qext (pnp): Rext is connected between the input terminal of the regulator and the base/emitter of Qext so that Qext turns on when the current through the regulator (and Rext) makes VRext = 0.7 V; the load current is IL = Iext + Imax.

problems.text: What value of R1 is necessary in a 7805 regulator to provide a constant current of 0.5 A to a variable load that can be adjusted from 1 Ω to 10 Ω?
problems.how: The 7805 holds 5 V between its output and ground terminals, so the current-setting resistor is R1 = 5 V/IL (neglecting IG).
assume: The regulator ground-terminal current IG is neglected.

problems.text: The input of a certain regulator increases by 3.5 V. As a result, the output voltage increases by 0.42 V. The nominal output is 20 V. Determine the regulation in %/V.
problems.ctx: Example 17–1: When the ac input voltage of a certain power supply changes, the input to the voltage regulator decreases by 5 V as a result, and the output of the regulator decreases by 0.25 V. The nominal output is 15 V. Determine the line regulation in %/V.
problems.how: Eq. 17–2 with ΔVOUT = 0.42 V, VOUT = 20 V, ΔVIN = 3.5 V.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.17 Related Problem of Example 17–1, p.853 (PDF 871)

problems.text: A regulator has a no-load output voltage of 18 V and a full-load output of 17.8 V at a load current of 50 mA. Determine the voltage regulation as a percentage change from no-load to full-load and also as a percentage change for each mA change in load current.
problems.ctx: Example 17–2: A certain voltage regulator has a 12 V output when there is no load (IL = 0).When there is a full-load current of 10 mA, the output voltage is 11.9 V. Express the voltage regulation as a percentage change from no-load to full-load and also as a percentage change for each mA change in load current.
problems.how: Eq. 17–3 with VNL = 18 V, VFL = 17.8 V, ΔIL = 50 mA.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.17 Related Problem of Example 17–2, p.854 (PDF 872)

problems.text: The following changes are made in the circuit in Figure 17–7: A 3.3 V zener replaces the 5.1 V zener, R1 = 1.8 kΩ, R2 = 22 kΩ, and R3 = 18 kΩ. What is the output voltage?
problems.ctx: Example 17–3: Determine the output voltage for the regulator in Figure 17–7.
problems.how: Series regulator: the op-amp keeps the voltage at the divider R2/R3 equal to the zener voltage, so VOUT = (1 + R2/R3)·VREF = (1 + 22/18) × 3.3 V (Floyd Eq. 17–3, Example 17–3 gives 10.2 V for 5.1 V and equal resistors).
assume: R1 only sets the zener current (6.5 mA), which is enough to keep the zener in breakdown.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.17 Related Problem of Example 17–3, p.858 (PDF 876)
problems.circuit: Figure 17–7 (p.857): series voltage regulator with an op-amp: the 5.1 V zener D1 (fed from VIN = +15 V through R1 = 1.0 kΩ) is the reference VREF on the + input; the pass transistor Q1 is driven by the op-amp; the feedback divider R2 = 10 kΩ (output to − input) and R3 = 10 kΩ (− input to ground). VOUT = (1 + R2/R3)·VREF (book result 10.2 V).

problems.text: In Figure 17–15, R1 is changed to 33 Ω. What must be the power rating of R1 if the maximum input voltage is 24 V?
problems.ctx: Example 17–5: In Figure 17–15, what power rating must R1 have if the maximum input voltage is 12.5 V?
answer: Power in R1: PR1 = VIN²/R1 (output shorted)
17.5 W → use a resistor rated at least 20 W
problems.how: Worst case again VOUT = 0: PR1 = 24²/33 Ω = 17.5 W; the next standard rating is 20 W (the printed answer to Problem 15, same method: 6.25 W for 25 V across 100 Ω).
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.17 Related Problem of Example 17–5, p.863 (PDF 881)
problems.circuit: Figure 17–15 (p.862): series regulator with current limiting: R1 = 22 Ω in series with the input (VIN to the output), the pass transistor Q1 with R2 = 1.0 kΩ, R3 = 10 kΩ and R4 = 10 kΩ; the worst case for R1 is a short-circuited output (VOUT = 0), when all of VIN appears across R1.

problems.text: What is the output voltage of the regulator if R2 is set at 2 kΩ?
problems.ctx: Example 17–6: Determine the minimum and maximum output voltages for the voltage regulator in Figure 17–30. Assume IADJ = 50 μA.
problems.how: LM317 output (Floyd §17–4).
assume: R1 = 220 Ω (Figure 17–30), IADJ = 50 μA as in Example 17–6.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.17 Related Problem of Example 17–6, p.872 (PDF 890)

problems.text: If Rext is changed to 1.5 Ω, at what current value will Qext turn on?
problems.ctx: Example 17–7: What value is Rext if the maximum current to be handled internally by the voltage regulator in Figure 17–34 is set at 700 mA?
answer: Qext turns on at IREG = 0.7 V/Rext
problems.how: The external pass transistor turns on when the drop across Rext reaches 0.7 V.
assume: VBE(on) = 0.7 V.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.17 Related Problem of Example 17–7, p.876 (PDF 894)

problems.text: If a 7808 regulator is used instead of the 7805, to what value would you change R1 to maintain a constant current of 0.5 A?
problems.ctx: Example 17–9: What value of R1 is necessary in a 7805 regulator to provide a constant current of 0.5 A to a variable load that can be adjusted from 1 Ω to 10 Ω?
problems.how: A 7808 holds 8 V across R1.
assume: IG neglected.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.17 Related Problem of Example 17–9, p.879 (PDF 897)

problems.text: The input of a certain regulator increases by 3.5 V. As a result, the output voltage increases by 0.042 V. The nominal output is 20 V. Determine the line regulation in both % and in %/V.
problems.how: Floyd Eq. 17–1 and 17–2.

problems.text: If a 5.0 V power supply has an output resistance of 80 mΩ and a specified maximum output current of 1.0 A, what is the load regulation? Give the result as a % and as a %/mA.
problems.how: Thevenin model of the supply: VFL = VNL − IFL·ROUT; load regulation from Eq. 17–3.
assume: The 5.0 V is the no-load voltage VNL and 1.0 A is the full-load current.

problems.text: A certain series regulator has an output voltage of 8 V. If the op-amp’s closed loop gain is 4, what is the value of the reference voltage?
problems.how: Series regulator: VOUT = Acl·VREF with Acl = 1 + R2/R3 (Floyd §17–2), so VREF = 8 V/4.

problems.text: With a constant input voltage of 17 V, the load resistance in Figure 17–48 is varied from 1 kΩ to 1.2 kΩ. Neglecting any change in output voltage, how much does the shunt current through Q1 change?
answer: Shunt current: IQ1 = (VIN − VOUT)/R1 − IL − I(R3 + R4); with VOUT, R1 and the divider unchanged, ΔIQ1 = −ΔIL
IL falls from VOUT/1 kΩ to VOUT/1.2 kΩ, so IQ1 INCREASES by VOUT·(1/1 kΩ − 1/1.2 kΩ) = VOUT/6 kΩ
For the regulated value VOUT = 5.1 V(1 + R3/R4) = 18.2 V
problems.how: Shunt regulator: Q1 takes the current that the load does not (Floyd §17–3); the series current through R1 is fixed when VIN and VOUT are fixed. The change in shunt current equals the decrease of the load current, ≈ 3 mA.
assume: The design output of this circuit is 5.1 V × (10 kΩ + 3.9 kΩ)/3.9 kΩ = 18.18 V, which is higher than the 17 V input in the statement (the regulator could not reach it); so the numbers above are given for both VOUT = 17 V and 18.2 V. The change is about 3 mA either way.
R1 = 100 Ω is confirmed by the printed answers of Problems 13 (1 V/100 Ω = 10 mA) and 15 (25 V/100 Ω = 250 mA, 6.25 W).
problems.circuit: Figure 17–48 (p.890): shunt voltage regulator: R1 = 100 Ω in series between VIN and VOUT; the shunt transistor Q1 (collector at VOUT, emitter to ground) is driven by an op-amp whose − input is the 5.1 V zener (fed by R2 = 12 kΩ from VIN) and whose + input is the divider R3 = 10 kΩ (from VOUT) and R4 = 3.9 kΩ (to ground); the load is the variable RL.

problems.text: A basic switching regulator is shown in Figure 17–49. If the switching frequency of the transistor is 10 kHz with an off-time of 60 μs, what is the output voltage?
answer: Period T = 1/f and on-time ton = T − toff
VOUT = D·VIN (average of the chopped input)
problems.how: Step-down switching regulator (Floyd §17–4): the inductor/capacitor filter averages the switched waveform, VOUT = (ton/T)·VIN = 0.4 × 12 V.
assume: Ideal switch and diode (no drops). The feedback network of the figure, 2.7 V × (10 kΩ + 15 kΩ)/15 kΩ = 4.5 V, is the voltage the loop would regulate to by adjusting ton; with the fixed 60 μs off-time given here the output is 4.8 V.
problems.circuit: Figure 17–49 (p.891): basic step-down switching regulator: +12 V input, series MOSFET Q1 driven by a modulator (f0 = 10 kHz, toff = 60 μs), freewheeling diode D1, inductor L, output capacitor C, load RL; the feedback divider R2 = 10 kΩ and R3 = 15 kΩ is compared with the 2.7 V zener D2 (fed through R1 = 4.7 kΩ) to set the pulse width.

problems.text: Determine the minimum and maximum output voltages for the circuit in Figure 17–52. IADJ = 50 μA.
answer: Maximum output (R2 = 10 kΩ): −[1.25 V(1 + R2/R1) + IADJ·R2]
problems.how: The LM337 is the negative counterpart of the LM317 (Floyd §17–5): the same formula applies to the magnitude, with the output negative. The input of −35 V is more negative than −28.4 V by enough margin.
assume: The sign convention of IADJ for the LM337 is taken as for the LM317 (it adds to the drop in R2), as in Example 17–6.
problems.circuit: Figure 17–52 (p.893): LM337 negative adjustable regulator: input −35 V; R1 = 470 Ω between the output and the adjustment terminal; R2 = 10 kΩ potentiometer from the adjustment terminal to ground. |VOUT| = 1.25 V(1 + R2/R1) + IADJ·R2.

problems.text: Using a 7812 voltage regulator and a 10 Ω load in Figure 17–53, how much power will the external pass transistor have to dissipate? The maximum internal regulator current is set at 500 mA by Rext.
answer: Power in Qext: Pext = Iext(VIN − VOUT)
problems.how: Floyd Example 17–8 method: Qext carries the part of the load current that the regulator does not (1.2 A − 0.5 A) and drops VIN − VOUT = 15 V − 12 V = 3 V.
assume: The input voltage 15 V is read from Figure 17–53 (the 7812 needs a few volts more than 12 V, which 15 V gives).
problems.circuit: Figure 17–53 (p.894): fixed regulator (7809 in the figure; a 7812 in Problem 26) with an external pass transistor Qext and Rext as in Figure 17–34, input +15 V, output decoupling C2.

problems.text: Using an LM317, design a circuit that will provide a constant current of 500 mA to a load.
problems.how: LM317 as a current regulator: IL = VREF/R1 (+ IADJ), with VREF = 1.25 V; the load goes where RL normally sits and R1 is the only resistor.
assume: IADJ (≈ 50 μA) is neglected.
